title: 06 · Estimating a Density in Many Dimensions
section: 3. Estimate the precision, not the covariance
text:
3. Estimate the precision, not the covariance
The move that rescues this is to change the target. Instead of estimating \(\Sigma\) and inverting it, estimate \(\Theta = \Sigma^{-1}\) directly. Three reasons, and the third is the real one.
It is the natural parameter. We already saw the likelihood is concave in \(\Theta\) and linear in \(S\). Penalised versions stay convex.
Inverting a bad estimate is worse than estimating the inverse. Small eigenvalues of \(S\) — and when \(n < p\), some are exactly zero — become enormous eigenvalues of \(S^{-1}\). Inversion amplifies precisely the directions the data constrains least.
Zeros in \(\Theta\) mean conditional independence. This is the fact that makes the whole programme work. For a Gaussian,
\[
\boxed{\;\Theta_{ij} = 0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
X_i \perp\!\!\!\perp X_j \;\big|\; X_{\setminus\{i,j\}}. \;}
\]
More precisely, the partial correlation — the correlation between \(X_i\) and \(X_j\) once every other variable has been regressed out — is read straight off the precision matrix:
\[
\rho_{ij \,\mid\, \text{rest}} \;=\; \frac{-\Theta_{ij}}{\sqrt{\Theta_{ii}\Theta_{jj}}}.
\]
An example worth carrying. Take three variables with an AR(1) correlation structure, \(\operatorname{corr}(X_i,X_j) = 0.6^{|i-j|}\):
\[
\Sigma = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0.6 & 0.36 \\ 0.6 & 1 & 0.6 \\ 0.36 & 0.6 & 1\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\Theta = \Sigma^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} 1.5625 & -0.9375 & 0 \\ -0.9375 & 2.125 & -0.9375 \\ 0 & -0.9375 & 1.5625 \end{pmatrix}.
\]
\(\Theta_{13} = 0\) exactly, and direct computation confirms \(\operatorname{Cov}(X_1, X_3 \mid X_2) = 0\). But the marginal correlation between \(X_1\) and \(X_3\) is \(0.36\), comfortably non-zero. The dependence is real; it is simply entirely mediated by \(X_2\). Covariance sees the association; precision sees whether it is direct.






The Gaussian graphical model



Draw a graph on \(p\) nodes with an edge between \(i\) and \(j\) whenever \(\Theta_{ij} \ne 0\). That graph is the conditional independence structure of the distribution — the Markov graph. For gene networks this is exactly the object of interest: an edge means “these two genes are associated even after accounting for all others”, which is the closest observational data gets to direct regulation.
The idea dates to Dempster’s covariance selection (1972). What changed in the 2000s was the ability to fit it when \(p \gg n\).


Sparsity as the assumption. A biologist will tell you each gene is regulated by a handful of others, not by twenty thousand. So assume most \(\Theta_{ij}\) are zero, and estimate under that assumption. Penalise with an \(\ell_1\) norm, which sets coefficients exactly to zero rather than merely shrinking them:
\[
\hat\Theta = \arg\max_{\Theta \succ 0}\;
\Big\{ \log\det\Theta - \operatorname{tr}(S\Theta) - \lambda \textstyle\sum_{i\ne j} |\Theta_{ij}| \Big\}.
\]
This is the graphical lasso (Yuan & Lin 2007; Banerjee et al. 2008; Friedman, Hastie & Tibshirani 2008). It is concave-plus-concave, so it is a convex problem with a unique solution — and crucially, for \(\lambda > 0\) the solution is positive definite even when \(S\) is singular. The penalty repairs the rank deficiency. A closely related route is neighbourhood selection (Meinshausen & Bühlmann 2006): run a lasso regression of each variable on all the others and patch the supports together.
The tuning parameter \(\lambda\) buys sparsity with bias, and choosing it is its own literature.

title: 06 · Estimating a Density in Many Dimensions
text:
4. The other structural assumptions
Sparsity of \(\Theta\) is one prior belief. It is not the only reasonable one, and the right one depends on what the coordinates are.








Assumption
Structure imposed
When it is reasonable




Sparse precision
most \(\Theta_{ij} = 0\)
networks; few direct interactions


Banded / tapered
\(\Sigma_{ij} \approx 0\) for \(|i-j|\) large
coordinates have an order — time, position along a genome


Thresholded
small entries of \(S\) set to zero
many negligible marginal associations


Shrinkage
\(\hat\Sigma = (1-\alpha)S + \alpha\, \tau I\)
no structural belief, just want invertibility


Factor model
\(\Sigma = BB^{\!\top} + D\), \(B\) tall and thin
a few latent drivers — finance, psychometrics


Low-rank + sparse
\(\Sigma = L + S\)
latent factors and local interactions


Isotropic / diagonal
\(\Sigma = \sigma^2 I\) or diagonal
the crude default; independence assumed



Shrinkage deserves a line of its own: the Ledoit–Wolf estimator (2004) mixes \(S\) with a scaled identity and chooses the mixing weight to minimise expected squared error. It assumes nothing about structure, always produces an invertible matrix, and is the sensible default when you have no scientific reason to prefer a shape. Banding and thresholding with rate guarantees are due to Bickel and Levina (2008).
The common thread. Every one of these replaces “estimate \(p(p+1)/2\) numbers” with “estimate far fewer, having assumed the rest away”. The assumption is doing the work. Its content is not statistical but scientific, and if it is wrong the estimate is confidently wrong.
crumbs: 06 · Estimating a Density in Many Dimensions

title: 06 · Estimating a Density in Many Dimensions
section: 5. One Gaussian is not enough: mixtures and EM
text:
5. One Gaussian is not enough: mixtures and EM
Real data is not unimodal. The next model up is a mixture of Gaussians:
\[
p(x) = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \pi_k\, \mathcal{N}(x; \mu_k, \Sigma_k),
\qquad \pi_k \ge 0, \ \textstyle\sum_k \pi_k = 1,
\]
which is exactly the latent-variable construction of note 03 — draw a component \(z \sim \text{Categorical}(\pi)\), then draw \(x \mid z \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_z,\Sigma_z)\), then forget \(z\). Mixtures are dense in a useful sense: with enough components you can approximate essentially any density.
The log-likelihood now contains a log of a sum, which does not separate, and there is no closed form. The standard tool is expectation–maximisation, which alternates:

E-step — compute the responsibility of component \(k\) for point \(i\), which is a posterior over the latent label by Bayes’ rule: \[
\gamma_{ik} = \frac{\pi_k\,\mathcal{N}(x_i;\mu_k,\Sigma_k)}{\sum_{m}\pi_m\,\mathcal{N}(x_i;\mu_m,\Sigma_m)};
\]
M-step — refit each component as if the responsibilities were the labels: \(\hat\pi_k = \frac1n\sum_i \gamma_{ik}\), \(\hat\mu_k = \frac{\sum_i \gamma_{ik}x_i}{\sum_i \gamma_{ik}}\), and similarly a responsibility-weighted covariance.

EM is coordinate ascent on a lower bound of the log-likelihood — the same ELBO that will reappear when we derive the diffusion training objective. It therefore increases the likelihood at every step, and converges to a stationary point.






Two failure modes worth knowing



Local optima. EM converges to a stationary point, not the global maximum, and different initialisations give different answers. Restart it.
The likelihood is unbounded. Put one component’s mean exactly on a data point and shrink its variance: the density at that point diverges, and so does the likelihood. At \(\sigma = 10^{-4}\) the peak density is already \(\approx 4000\). There is no maximum likelihood estimator for a Gaussian mixture — the supremum is \(+\infty\), attained by a degenerate spike. What EM finds is a well-behaved local maximum, and implementations add a variance floor or a prior to stay away from the cliff.


And the counting problem has not gone away: \(K\) full covariances cost \(K \cdot p(p+3)/2\) parameters. For MNIST with \(K=10\) that is over three million.
crumbs: 06 · Estimating a Density in Many Dimensions

title: 06 · Estimating a Density in Many Dimensions
section: 6. Give up on parameters: kernel density estimation
text:
6. Give up on parameters: kernel density estimation
The nonparametric alternative makes no assumption about shape at all. Put a small bump on every observation and add them up:
\[
\hat p_h(x) = \frac{1}{n h^p} \sum_{i=1}^{n} K\!\left(\frac{x - x_i}{h}\right).
\]
In one dimension this is excellent and its theory is complete. The bandwidth \(h\) trades bias against variance, and with the optimal choice the mean integrated squared error decays like
\[
\text{MISE} \;\asymp\; n^{-4/(p+4)}
\]
for a second-order kernel and a twice-differentiable density. Read the exponent. At \(p=1\) it is \(n^{-4/5}\), nearly the parametric \(n^{-1}\). As \(p\) grows it approaches \(n^{0}\) — no convergence at all.
Invert it and ask how many samples you need to match, in \(p\) dimensions, the accuracy that \(n = 100\) buys in one:



\(p\)
samples required




1
100


2
251


5
~4,000


10
~400,000


20
~\(4 \times 10^{9}\)


50
~\(4 \times 10^{21}\)


100
~\(4 \times 10^{41}\)



Interactive — The KDE Lab builds the estimate one kernel at a time, then lets you sweep \(h\) against a three-component Gaussian mixture and watch it fail in both directions. Its third panel plots the integrated squared error against \(h\): the curve is U-shaped, and its minimum slides left as \(n\) grows, which is \(h^\star \propto n^{-1/5}\) made visible.


At \(p = 100\) — still a small problem by modern standards — the requirement exceeds the number of atoms in the observable universe by a wide margin. This is not an artefact of KDE. It is a minimax lower bound: over the class of smooth densities, no estimator does better than \(n^{-2s/(2s+p)}\) for smoothness \(s\). The obstruction is information-theoretic, not algorithmic.






The curse of dimensionality, stated plainly



Local methods need neighbours, and in high dimension nothing has any. To capture a fraction \(f\) of the data in a hypercube you need side length \(f^{1/p}\): at \(p = 100\), capturing 1% of the data requires a cube spanning \(0.01^{1/100} =
0.955\) of the range of every coordinate. A “local” neighbourhood is nearly the entire space, so local averaging averages over everything and estimates nothing.
Every classical density estimator is local averaging in some disguise. They all inherit this.

title: 06 · Estimating a Density in Many Dimensions
text:
7. Another route entirely: be Bayesian
Everything so far produces a point estimate — one matrix, one mixture. The Bayesian alternative refuses to pick: put a prior on the parameters, condition on the data, and report the whole posterior.
Conjugacy makes the Gaussian case exact. With an inverse-Wishart prior \(\Sigma \sim \mathcal{IW}(\Psi,\nu)\), the posterior is again inverse-Wishart,
\[
\Sigma \mid x_{1:n} \;\sim\; \mathcal{IW}\big(\Psi + nS,\; \nu + n\big),
\]
and the posterior mean \((\Psi + nS)/(\nu + n - p - 1)\) is a shrinkage estimator — the sample covariance pulled toward the prior scale \(\Psi\). Compare §4: this is Ledoit–Wolf shrinkage, arrived at from a different direction.
Look at what that fixes. When \(n < p\), \(nS\) is singular. But \(\Psi\) is positive definite, so \(\Psi + nS\) is positive definite too, and the posterior is proper whenever \(\nu > p-1\). With \(p=8\), \(n=5\): the scatter matrix has rank 4, the posterior scale has rank 8, and the posterior mean is positive definite. The prior repairs the rank deficiency — not by penalising, but by supplying the information the data lacks. Which is exactly what a penalty does too, and that is not a coincidence:






Penalties are log-priors



Maximising \(\log p(\text{data} \mid \theta) - \lambda \|\theta\|_1\) is maximising \(\log p(\text{data}\mid\theta) + \log p(\theta)\) for a Laplace prior. The graphical lasso is the MAP estimate under a Laplace prior on the off-diagonal entries of \(\Theta\). Every penalty in §3–§4 has a prior behind it: ridge is Gaussian, lasso is Laplace, and the modern shrinkage priors — spike-and-slab, horseshoe — have no penalty analogue at all, which is part of their appeal.


Sparsity, done properly. A spike-and-slab prior puts an atom at zero on each \(\Theta_{ij}\), so the posterior assigns genuine probability to each graph. Instead of one estimated network you get a distribution over networks, and the posterior inclusion probability of an edge is a direct answer to “is this regulatory link real?”.
Nonparametric Bayes. A Dirichlet process mixture of Gaussians is a mixture with infinitely many components, of which finitely many are ever used. It removes the need to choose \(K\) in §5 — the number of clusters is inferred rather than tuned.
The cost is computation. Outside conjugate cases the posterior is intractable, so it is explored by Markov chain Monte Carlo: construct a chain whose stationary distribution is the posterior and run it. Gibbs sampling for conditionally conjugate blocks, Metropolis–Hastings in general, Hamiltonian Monte Carlo and NUTS when gradients are available. Variational inference is the cheaper approximation, trading exactness for speed.






What Bayes buys, and what it does not



Buys: honest uncertainty. A credible interval on every entry of \(\Theta\), a posterior probability for every edge, automatic regularisation, and no cross-validation for \(\lambda\) — give it a hyperprior and integrate it out. For a scientific question like “which of these edges would survive more data?” this is the right tool and the penalised point estimate simply cannot answer.
Does not buy: escape from the curse. MCMC mixes slowly in high dimension, the space of graphs is combinatorial, and convergence is genuinely hard to certify. At \(p = 20{,}000\) it is not a contender. The difficulty has moved from statistics to computation, but it has not gone away.








MCMC is closer to this course than it looks



An MCMC sampler draws from a distribution it can only evaluate up to a normalising constant — which is precisely the obstacle that makes density estimation hard. One such sampler, Langevin dynamics, updates
\[
x \;\leftarrow\; x + \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}\,\nabla_x \log p(x) + \sqrt{\varepsilon}\, z,
\qquad z \sim \mathcal{N}(0,I),
\]
and notice what it needs: only \(\nabla_x \log p(x)\), the score. The normalising constant differentiates away. This is the same score that appeared in note 01 via Tweedie’s formula, and the same object Module 4 will learn from data.
Score-based generative models are, genealogically, MCMC with a learned score. The line from this section to the end of the course is short.

title: 06 · Estimating a Density in Many Dimensions
text:
8. Sampling without estimating the density
Notice what the MCMC of §7 quietly achieved. It produced draws from a posterior nobody could write down, and at no point did it build an estimate of that posterior. That distinction is the hinge of this whole note: estimating a density and sampling from one are different problems, and the second is very often the easier of the two. Generation only ever needed the second.
Two classical algorithms make the point, and both need the target only up to a normalising constant — which is exactly the part that is unobtainable.

Rejection sampling: propose, then judge
Pick a proposal \(q\) you can sample, and a constant \(M\) with \(p(x) \le M\,q(x)\) for every \(x\). Then repeat: draw \(x \sim q\) and \(u \sim \mathrm{Uniform}(0,1)\), and accept \(x\) if
\[
u \;<\; \frac{p(x)}{M\,q(x)} .
\]
Accepted draws are distributed exactly as \(p\) — not approximately. The proof is one line: the pair \((x, u\,M q(x))\) is uniform under the envelope \(Mq\), and accepting keeps precisely those falling under \(p\), so the survivors are uniform under \(p\), whose \(x\)-marginal is \(p\). The acceptance rate is \(1/M\).
The Bayesian case is the tidy one. Take the prior as the proposal and note that the posterior is \(p(x) \propto q(x) L(x)\) for a likelihood \(L\). If \(L\) is bounded then \(M = \max L / Z\) works, the ratio collapses, and the rule becomes
\[
\text{accept with probability } \frac{L(x)}{\max L} .
\]
No normalising constant, no evidence integral, no density estimate — just the likelihood evaluated at a point.






The envelope must actually exist



It is easy to write down a proposal for which no valid \(M\) exists. Take target \(\mathcal{N}(-1,1)\) and proposal \(\mathcal{N}(0,1)\): the ratio is
\[
\frac{p(x)}{q(x)} = e^{-x-\frac12} \;\xrightarrow[x\to-\infty]{}\; \infty ,
\]
so \(\sup_x p/q = \infty\) and rejection sampling is simply unavailable. A proposal must have heavier tails than the target in every direction. Shifting a Gaussian is not enough; you have to widen it.


And then the usual wall. Take target \(\mathcal{N}(0,I_d)\) with a proposal \(\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2 I_d)\), \(\sigma > 1\). The optimal constant is \(M = \sigma^{d}\), so the acceptance rate is \(\sigma^{-d}\):



\(d\)

\(7 \times 10^{-5}\)
\(2 \times 10^{-18}\)



A proposal ten percent too wide is already useless at \(d = 100\). Rejection sampling is exact and, in high dimension, exactly worthless.


MCMC: stop proposing from scratch, and walk
The fix is to stop drawing independently and instead move from where you already are. Gibbs sampling draws each coordinate from its conditional given the others; Metropolis–Hastings proposes a local step and accepts with a ratio. Both need \(p\) only through ratios, so the constant cancels again.
What you buy is that the samples are no longer wasted. What you pay is that they are no longer independent — consecutive draws are correlated, and the chain must run a while before its distribution resembles the target at all.
That last phrase deserves to be taken literally. For Gibbs on a standard bivariate normal with correlation \(\rho\), the \(x\)-coordinate is exactly an AR(1) process with coefficient \(\rho^2\), and the law of the chain at step \(t\) started from \(x_0\) is available in closed form:
\[
\boxed{\;x_t \mid x_0 \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}\big(\rho^{2t} x_0,\; 1 - \rho^{4t}\big).\;}
\]
The mean decays geometrically toward \(0\) and the variance climbs toward \(1\). So there is not one distribution here but a sequence of them, \(p_0, p_1, p_2,
\dots\), flowing toward \(p_\infty\). Burn-in is the interval over which that flow is still visibly incomplete, and the lag-1 autocorrelation \(\rho^2\) is why a strongly correlated target mixes slowly.
Interactive — The Sampling Lab runs both algorithms: darts under an envelope for rejection, and for Gibbs a staircase walk, a trace plot, and 4,000 parallel chains whose histogram at step \(t\) is drawn against the exact \(p_t\) above.








A chain is a time series, and its law obeys a PDE



\(p_t \to p_\infty\) is the discrete-time shadow of the Fokker–Planck equation of Module 5, which describes exactly this: how a density evolves under stochastic dynamics. The continuous-time version of the walk is Langevin dynamics, and as §7 noted it needs only the score \(\nabla_x \log p\).
A diffusion model is this picture used deliberately. Its forward process is a chain run in the easy direction — toward a known Gaussian, no learning required. Its reverse process is the same flow run backwards, which is the hard direction and the one worth a semester.




The proposal is a generator; the test is a discriminator
Look at rejection sampling structurally rather than procedurally. It has exactly two components: something that produces candidates, and something that judges them. That is the architecture of a generative adversarial network, with the proposal in the role of the generator and the acceptance test in the role of the discriminator.
The parallel is not a loose analogy — both are density-ratio methods. The optimal discriminator for a GAN with generator distribution \(p_g\) is
\[
D^{*}(x) = \frac{p_{\text{data}}(x)}{p_{\text{data}}(x) + p_g(x)} = \frac{r(x)}{1 + r(x)},
\qquad r = \frac{p_{\text{data}}}{p_g},
\]
a strictly increasing function of the ratio \(r\). Rejection sampling accepts with probability \(p(x)/(M q(x))\) — the same ratio, differently scaled. Both machines run on \(p/q\); they differ in what they know about it and what they do with it.

The decisive difference is in the row about rejected mass. Rejection sampling throws a dart away and learns nothing; a GAN turns every failure into a signal telling the generator which way to go. That is what makes one method collapse in high dimension and the other not.






The real limitation, in both classical methods



In rejection sampling the proposal \(q\) is chosen for convenience. In Metropolis–Hastings the proposal kernel is chosen for convenience. In Gibbs the “proposal” is whatever conditionals happen to be tractable. In every case a human picks a distribution because it is easy to sample, and then hopes it resembles the target — and in high dimension it does not, which is precisely the \(\sigma^{-d}\) table above.
Modern generative models remove that choice: the proposal is learned. A GAN learns a generator, a flow learns an invertible map, and a diffusion model learns a reverse process. Each replaces a hand-picked proposal with one fitted to the data.
A diffusion model goes one step further and dispenses with the judge entirely. Because the forward process is a sequence of small Gaussian steps, each reverse step is nearly Gaussian and can be matched directly — there is nothing to accept or reject. The convenience-chosen proposal, the wasted draws, and the adversarial referee all disappear at once. That is the destination of this course.

section: 9. Where this sits in the landscape
text:
9. Where this sits in the landscape
Everything above is unsupervised: there are no labels, only \(x\)’s, and the goal is the distribution itself. It is worth naming what else lives here and what lives next door, because the difficulty is not the same.
Other unsupervised problems. Clustering — partition the data, which is a Gaussian mixture with hard assignments (\(k\)-means is EM with spherical components and responsibilities rounded to 0/1). Dimension reduction — PCA is the factor model of §4 read as an estimator; manifold learning is its nonlinear cousin. Latent variable modelling — factor analysis, topic models, and eventually VAEs. Anomaly detection — density estimation with a threshold on the output.
Supervised problems, by contrast, estimate a conditional: regression wants \(\mathbb{E}[y \mid x]\), classification wants \(\mathbb{P}(y \mid x)\). These are easier, and it is worth being precise about why: you need one number per input rather than a normalised function over the whole space, there is a label telling you when you are wrong, and you never have to compute a normalising constant. A classifier can be excellent while knowing nothing about \(p(x)\).
This course stays in unsupervised density estimation, because generation demands the full distribution. You cannot sample from a conditional mean.

title: 06 · Estimating a Density in Many Dimensions
section: 10. Why this was hard, and what actually solved it
text:
10. Why this was hard, and what actually solved it
Roughly 2000–2010 was an extraordinarily active decade on precisely this problem. Sparsity, \(\ell_1\) penalties, oracle inequalities, minimax rates over structured classes, the graphical lasso, compressed sensing. It produced beautiful and permanent mathematics, and it did not produce a model that can generate a photograph.
Why not. The classical programme’s answer to \(n \ll p\) was: impose structure you can write down and verify. Sparse. Banded. Low-rank. Those are strong assumptions, deliberately simple so that theorems are provable and parameters interpretable. But the structure in a natural image is not sparsity in pixel covariance. It is edges composing into textures composing into objects — a deep, nonlinear, compositional structure that no one can write as a constraint on a matrix. Classical methods were limited not by their estimators but by the poverty of the structures they could express.
What deep learning changed — four moves, none of which is “more data” alone:

Learn the structure instead of assuming it. A network’s layers are a parametrisation of compositional structure. You do not have to know the shape of the dependence; you fit it.
Stop evaluating the density. KDE estimates \(p(x)\) at points, and that is what the curse taxes. Modern generative models never do. A GAN or a flow learns a map from noise to data; a diffusion model learns the score \(\nabla_x \log p(x)\). Learning a map is a supervised-flavoured regression problem, and it dodges the normalising constant entirely.
Exploit the manifold. Real data occupies a thin, curved, low-dimensional subset of its ambient space. That is exactly the singular case of note 05 where the density does not exist — fatal for classical estimation, harmless for a model that only has to produce samples on the manifold.
Amortise. Parameters are shared across all inputs by a single network, so the parameter count grows with model size rather than with \(p^2\).

The two-point model of note 01 is the seed of this: it never wrote down \(p_\text{data}\): it learned the map \(\mathbb{E}[x_0 \mid x_\sigma]\) and integrated.






What statistics still has that deep learning does not



The honest accounting runs both ways. Ask a diffusion model which genes regulate which and it has no answer — it produces samples, not a graph, and offers no \(p\)-value, no confidence set, no testable conditional independence. The graphical lasso answers exactly that question, with guarantees.
They optimise different objectives. Statistics wanted interpretable, verifiable structure in a regime with almost no data. Deep learning wanted samples that look right, given a great deal of it. Deep learning did not solve the classical problem; it found a version of the problem where the curse of dimensionality is not the binding constraint, and solved that instead.
Knowing which question you are asking is the whole skill.

title: 06 · Estimating a Density in Many Dimensions
section: 11. The bridge: from describing to comparing
text:
11. The bridge: from describing to comparing
Every method above tried to write down \(p_\text{data}\) — as a Gaussian, a sparse graphical model, a mixture, a sum of kernels, a posterior. All of them hit the same wall from different sides.
So change the question. And the surprise is that we have already been asking the new one without noticing.
Maximum likelihood was always a comparison. Take the average log-likelihood and let \(n\) grow; by the law of large numbers it converges to an expectation under the true distribution:
\[
\frac1n \sum_{i=1}^{n} \log p_\theta(x_i)
\;\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}\;
\mathbb{E}_{p_\text{data}}\big[\log p_\theta(X)\big].
\]
Now add and subtract \(\mathbb{E}_{p_\text{data}}[\log p_\text{data}(X)]\):
\[
\mathbb{E}_{p_\text{data}}\big[\log p_\theta\big]
= \underbrace{-\,H(p_\text{data})}_{\text{does not involve } \theta}
\;-\; \mathrm{KL}\big(p_\text{data} \,\|\, p_\theta\big).
\]
The entropy term is a constant as far as \(\theta\) is concerned. Therefore
\[
\boxed{\;\arg\max_\theta \ \text{likelihood}
\;=\; \arg\min_\theta \ \mathrm{KL}\big(p_\text{data} \,\|\, p_\theta\big).\;}
\]
(Check it numerically: over a grid of candidate means, average log-likelihood plus KL is constant to sampling error, and the two optima coincide exactly.)
Fitting was never “describe the data”. It was “get close to the data distribution”. We just never had to name the notion of closeness, because likelihood chose one for us.
Naming it is the pivot, because it exposes a choice we did not know we were making. If “fit” means “make \(p_\theta\) close to \(p_\text{data}\)”, then: close in what sense? And some senses do not require a density at all — which is exactly the escape route, since the density is the thing we cannot get.
Three ways KL specifically fails us.

It needs densities. \(\mathrm{KL}(p\|q) = \int p \log(p/q)\) is meaningless unless both have densities. On a manifold — the situation of §8 and of real image data — \(p_\text{data}\) has no density with respect to Lebesgue measure, and the definition does not apply.
Disjoint supports send it to infinity. If \(p_\theta\) puts no mass where \(p_\text{data}\) lives, \(\mathrm{KL} = \infty\). Two distributions on nearby but non-overlapping manifolds are infinitely far apart no matter how nearly they touch — and infinity has no useful gradient. A model initialised anywhere sensible gets no signal telling it which way to move.
It is asymmetric, and the two orders behave differently: \(\mathrm{KL}(p_\text{data}\|p_\theta)\) is mode-covering and punishes missing mass; \(\mathrm{KL}(p_\theta\|p_\text{data})\) is mode-seeking and punishes spurious mass. Neither is “the” distance.

What we want instead is a comparison that stays finite between distributions with disjoint support, and degrades gracefully as they separate — one that measures how far the mass must move, not whether the supports overlap. That is the Wasserstein distance, and it is the reason WGAN replaced the original GAN objective.






What the next note does



It turns out the sensible comparisons fall into two families, meeting in almost one place:

\(f\)-divergences — KL, reverse KL, Jensen–Shannon, \(\chi^2\), total variation. Built by integrating a convex function of the density ratio, so they all need densities and all suffer failure (1) and (2) above.
Integral probability metrics — Wasserstein, MMD, total variation. Built by maximising a difference of expectations over a class of test functions, so they need only the ability to draw samples.

Total variation is the one distribution in both families. Wasserstein is an IPM and is not an \(f\)-divergence — which is precisely why it survives disjoint supports where every \(f\)-divergence saturates.
That is note 07. Once you can measure the gap between two distributions without writing either of them down, you can train a generative model — and the rest of this course is the construction of one particular, very well-behaved way of doing so.

title: 07 · Comparing Distributions: From CDFs to KL, and the Two Families
text:
1. In one dimension, compare the CDFs
Two distributions \(P\) and \(Q\) on \(\mathbb{R}\), with CDFs \(F\) and \(G\). The CDF determines the distribution completely, so any honest measure of “how different are \(P\) and \(Q\)” can be read off the gap
\[
\Delta(x) \;=\; F(x) - G(x).
\]
That is a function. To turn a function into a single number you take a norm — and the three standard choices give three quantities you have already met or are about to.
\[
\underbrace{\sup_x |\Delta(x)|}_{\textbf{Kolmogorov–Smirnov}}
\qquad
\underbrace{\int |\Delta(x)|\,dx}_{\textbf{Wasserstein-1}}
\qquad
\underbrace{\int \Delta(x)^2\,w(x)\,dx}_{\textbf{Cramér–von Mises}}
\]
The \(L^\infty\), \(L^1\) and \(L^2\) norms of one object. That is the whole taxonomy of one-dimensional distances-between-CDFs.
crumbs: 07 · Comparing Distributions: From CDFs to KL, and the Two Families

title: 07 · Comparing Distributions: From CDFs to KL, and the Two Families
text:
The Kolmogorov–Smirnov statistic
\[
D(P,Q) \;=\; \sup_x \big| F(x) - G(x) \big| .
\]
The largest vertical gap between the two CDF curves. It is always in \([0,1]\), it is a genuine metric, and it is distribution-free in a useful sense: if you replace \(P\) by any strictly increasing transformation of itself and do the same to \(Q\), \(D\) does not change — because relabelling the axis slides both curves identically. That invariance is why the KS test has a universal critical value table that does not depend on what you are testing.
Its empirical version is what you would actually compute: replace \(F\) by the empirical CDF \(\hat F_n(x) = \frac1n\#\{i : x_i \le x\}\), a staircase with a step of \(1/n\) at each sample, and take the sup — which is attained at one of the data points, so it is a finite maximum.
For \(P = \mathcal{N}(0,1)\) and \(Q = \mathcal{N}(\mu,1)\) the sup sits at \(x=\mu/2\) by symmetry, giving \(D = 2\Phi(\mu/2) - 1\): \(0.197\) at \(\mu = 0.5\), \(0.383\) at \(\mu=1\), \(0.954\) at \(\mu = 4\). Notice how it saturates — by \(\mu = 4\) it has nearly exhausted its range and can barely distinguish \(\mu = 4\) from \(\mu = 40\).


The \(L^1\) norm is a transport cost
Take the same gap and integrate its absolute value instead of maximising it:
\[
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \big| F(x) - G(x)\big|\,dx \;=\; W_1(P,Q),
\]
the Wasserstein-1 distance — and this is exactly the quantity Transport You Can Compute derives as the cheapest way to move the mass of \(P\) onto \(Q\) when moving a unit of mass a distance \(|x-y|\) costs \(|x-y|\). The area between the CDF curves is the transport bill.
So the bridge to transport is not an analogy. In one dimension the optimal transport cost and an \(L^1\) norm of the CDF gap are the same number, and the monotone (quantile) coupling is what achieves it.
Unlike KS, \(W_1\) does not saturate: for \(\mathcal{N}(0,1)\) against \(\mathcal{N}(\mu,1)\) it equals exactly \(|\mu|\), growing without bound. It answers “how far?” rather than “how distinguishable?”, and that difference will turn out to matter a great deal in §6.


And the \(L^2\) norm
\(\int (F-G)^2 w\,dx\) gives the Cramér–von Mises family; with the weight \(w = 1/(G(1-G))\) it is the Anderson–Darling statistic, which up-weights the tails and is correspondingly better at detecting differences out there. These are goodness-of-fit tools rather than modelling objectives, so we will not use them further — but they belong on the map.


Histograms: the same story, discretised
For distributions on a finite ordered set of bins, the integral becomes a sum and \(W_1\) becomes the Earth Mover’s Distance: \(W_1(p,q) = \sum_k |F_p(k) - F_q(k)|\), which is the discrete transport problem of tutorial 09 — solvable exactly as a min-cost flow, with the Transport Plan Lab to play with.






Where this whole approach stops working



Every construction above needs a CDF, and a CDF needs the real line to be ordered — \(F(x) = \mathbb{P}(X \le x)\) has no meaning without \(\le\). In \(\mathbb{R}^d\) there is no canonical order, no canonical CDF, and no canonical “area between the curves”.
Transport survives, because a cost \(c(x,y)\) makes sense in any dimension — but the closed form is gone and you are solving an optimisation. What we need instead is a way to compare distributions pointwise, using only the values of the two densities at the same point and never their order. That is KL.
crumbs: 07 · Comparing Distributions: From CDFs to KL, and the Two Families

title: 07 · Comparing Distributions: From CDFs to KL, and the Two Families
text:
2. KL divergence
For distributions with densities \(p\) and \(q\),
\[
\boxed{\;\mathrm{KL}(p \,\|\, q) \;=\; \int p(x)\,\log\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}\,dx
\;=\; \mathbb{E}_{x\sim p}\!\left[\log\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}\right].\;}
\]
No ordering, no CDF, no dimension limit: it compares the two densities at each point, through their ratio, and averages the log-ratio under \(p\).
It is non-negative, \(\mathrm{KL}(p\|q) \ge 0\) with equality only when \(p = q\) almost everywhere. This is Jensen from the inequalities tutorial: \(-\log\) is convex, so
\[
\mathrm{KL}(p\|q) = \mathbb{E}_p\!\left[-\log\frac{q}{p}\right]
\;\ge\; -\log \mathbb{E}_p\!\left[\frac{q}{p}\right] = -\log\!\int q = 0 .
\]
It is not a metric. It is asymmetric, \(\mathrm{KL}(p\|q) \neq \mathrm{KL}(q\|p)\), and fails the triangle inequality. Hence divergence, not distance.
It is infinite when supports disagree. If \(p(x) > 0\) somewhere \(q(x) = 0\), the integrand is \(+\infty\). This is not a technicality — §6 is about the consequences.
Gaussian closed form, which is why this course can compute with it:
\[
\mathrm{KL}\big(\mathcal{N}(\mu_1,\sigma_1^2)\,\big\|\,\mathcal{N}(\mu_2,\sigma_2^2)\big)
= \log\frac{\sigma_2}{\sigma_1} + \frac{\sigma_1^2 + (\mu_1-\mu_2)^2}{2\sigma_2^2} - \frac12 .
\]
With equal variances this collapses to \((\mu_1-\mu_2)^2/2\sigma^2\) — a squared distance. Every KL term in a diffusion model’s training objective is an instance of this formula, which is the reason the objective reduces to a sum of squared errors.

title: 07 · Comparing Distributions: From CDFs to KL, and the Two Families
section: 3. KL is maximum likelihood in disguise
text:
3. KL is maximum likelihood in disguise
This is the connection that makes KL more than one option among many.
Let \(p_{\text{data}}\) be the true distribution and \(p_\theta\) your model. Expand:
\[
\mathrm{KL}(p_{\text{data}} \,\|\, p_\theta)
= \underbrace{\int p_{\text{data}}\log p_{\text{data}}}_{-H(p_{\text{data}}),\ \text{no } \theta}
\;-\; \int p_{\text{data}}\log p_\theta .
\]
The first term does not involve \(\theta\) at all. So
\[
\arg\min_\theta \mathrm{KL}(p_{\text{data}}\|p_\theta)
= \arg\max_\theta \; \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_{\text{data}}}\big[\log p_\theta(x)\big],
\]
and replacing the expectation by its sample average over \(x_1,\dots,x_n\) gives
\[
\arg\max_\theta \;\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \log p_\theta(x_i),
\]
which is exactly the maximum likelihood estimator of Distributions and Maximum Likelihood.






The sentence to remember



Maximum likelihood is minimising the forward KL from the data distribution to the model. Every time you fit by MLE — the Gaussian fit, logistic regression via BCE, a normalizing flow — you are minimising \(\mathrm{KL}(p_{\text{data}}\|p_\theta)\) whether or not anyone says so. The empirical average is just the Monte Carlo estimate of an integral you never write down.



Which way round? Forward and reverse KL behave differently
Because KL is asymmetric, the two directions optimise for different things.









\(\mathrm{KL}(p_{\text{data}}\|p_\theta)\) — forward
\(\mathrm{KL}(p_\theta\|p_{\text{data}})\) — reverse




Penalises
\(p_\theta\) small where data is
\(p_\theta\) large where data is not


Behaviour
mode-covering: spreads to cover all the data
mode-seeking: locks onto one mode


Failure mode
blurry averages over modes
ignores modes entirely


Used by
maximum likelihood, flows, diffusion bounds
variational inference, the VAE’s \(q\)



The forward direction cannot afford \(p_\theta \approx 0\) anywhere the data lives — the log ratio explodes — so it hedges and covers. The reverse direction is integrated under \(p_\theta\), so it simply avoids putting mass in the wrong place and is content to ignore parts of the target. This is exactly the single-Gaussian-fitted-to-a-mixture trap of tutorial 02, now with a name.
The gap is not subtle. Fit a single Gaussian to an equal mixture of \(\mathcal{N}(-2, 0.7^2)\) and \(\mathcal{N}(2, 0.7^2)\) and the two criteria give completely different answers, each of which the other criterion scores as terrible:

The forward optimum is exactly moment matching — for a Gaussian family, minimising \(\mathrm{KL}(p\|q)\) means matching the mean and variance of \(p\), which is why it lands between the modes where no data lives. The reverse optimum sits on a mode and is the same distance from either, so which one it finds depends entirely on where the optimiser starts.
Interactive — The KL Lab draws both optima together, shades the two integrands so you can see where each direction pays its penalty, and plots both objectives against \(\mu\): forward KL has a single basin, reverse KL has one per mode with a barrier between them.

4. KL is one of a family: the \(f\)-divergences
Fix a convex \(f\) with \(f(1) = 0\) and define
\[
D_f(p \,\|\, q) \;=\; \int q(x)\, f\!\left(\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}\right) dx .
\]
Convexity plus \(f(1)=0\) gives \(D_f \ge 0\) with equality at \(p=q\), by Jensen — the same one-line argument as for KL. Different \(f\), different divergence:

All of these share one structural feature, and it is the one that matters: they depend on \(p\) and \(q\) only through the pointwise ratio \(p/q\). They never look at where the points are. Move a lump of \(q\)’s mass from just beside \(p\) to a mile away and no \(f\)-divergence notices, because the ratio at every point is unchanged.

section: 5. Wasserstein, and what changes in more than one dimension
text:
5. Wasserstein, and what changes in more than one dimension
So far \(W_1\) has appeared only through its one-dimensional formula \(\int |F - G|\). That formula is a happy accident of the line, and it is worth being precise about what the general object is before relying on it.
The Kantorovich definition. For \(p \ge 1\) and distributions \(P, Q\) on \(\mathbb{R}^d\),
\[
W_p(P,Q) \;=\; \left( \inf_{\gamma \in \Pi(P,Q)}
\int \lVert x - y \rVert^{p} \, d\gamma(x,y) \right)^{1/p},
\]
where \(\Pi(P,Q)\) is the set of couplings — joint distributions on \(\mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{R}^d\) whose marginals are \(P\) and \(Q\). A coupling is a plan for moving mass; the integral is what the plan costs; \(W_p\) is the cost of the cheapest one. Nothing here mentions densities, which is exactly why it survives when densities do not exist.

Why one dimension is special
On the line there is a total order, and that changes everything. The optimal plan is forced to be monotone — cheapest transport never lets paths cross — and the monotone coupling is unique and explicit. It is the one matching quantile to quantile, which gives, for every \(p \ge 1\),
\[
W_p(P,Q) = \left( \int_0^1 \big| F^{-1}(u) - G^{-1}(u) \big|^{p} du \right)^{1/p} .
\]
Sort both samples, subtract, average. \(O(n \log n)\), and no optimisation at all. (Checked against an exact assignment solver on 3,000-point samples: the sorted matching reproduces the optimal cost to machine precision at \(p = 1, 2, 3\).)






The CDF formula is \(p = 1\) only



The quantile formula above holds for all \(p\). The other one-dimensional formula, the one in §1,
\[
W_1(P,Q) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \big| F(x) - G(x) \big| \, dx ,
\]
does not generalise. At \(p=1\) the area between the two CDFs happens to equal the area between the two quantile functions — the same region, measured along different axes — so the two expressions agree. For \(p > 1\) that coincidence breaks, and \(\big(\int |F-G|^p dx\big)^{1/p}\) is not \(W_p\) and is not any Wasserstein distance.
Concretely, for \(\mathcal{N}(0,1)\) against \(\mathcal{N}(1.5, 2^2)\):







quantity
value




\(\int_0^1 \lvert F^{-1}-G^{-1}\rvert\,du\)
1.5586


\(\int \lvert F-G\rvert\,dx\)
1.5586   (agree, as they must at \(p=1\))


\(W_2 = \big(\int_0^1 \lvert F^{-1}-G^{-1}\rvert^2 du\big)^{1/2}\)
1.8028


\(\big(\int \lvert F-G\rvert^2 dx\big)^{1/2}\)
0.6918   (not \(W_2\), not anything)



When in doubt, work with quantiles: that form is the one that generalises in \(p\). Neither form generalises in dimension, which is the subject of the rest of this section.


For one-dimensional Gaussians the quantile integral collapses to a formula worth remembering, and it is the \(d=1\) case of Bures–Wasserstein below:
\[
W_2\big(\mathcal{N}(\mu_1,\sigma_1^2),\ \mathcal{N}(\mu_2,\sigma_2^2)\big)
= \sqrt{(\mu_1-\mu_2)^2 + (\sigma_1-\sigma_2)^2} .
\]
(For the pair above: \(\sqrt{1.5^2 + 1^2} = 1.8028\), matching the numeric quantile integral.)
In \(\mathbb{R}^d\) with \(d > 1\) there is no total order, so this construction simply has nothing to stand on. There is no quantile function, and no reason a cheapest plan should be expressible in closed form. What survives is weaker but still substantial:

It is still a linear program. For empirical measures on \(n\) points each, the Kantorovich problem is an \(n \times n\) assignment problem. Exact solvers cost about \(O(n^3 \log n)\) — fine for thousands of points, hopeless for millions.
The dual still holds. Kantorovich–Rubinstein gives, for \(p = 1\), \(W_1 = \sup_{\lVert f \rVert_{\mathrm{Lip}} \le 1} \mathbb{E}_P[f] - \mathbb{E}_Q[f]\), which is what a WGAN critic estimates.
Brenier’s theorem replaces the quantile map. If \(P\) is absolutely continuous, the optimal \(p=2\) plan is deterministic: there is a map \(T\) with \(T_\# P = Q\) attaining the infimum, and it is the gradient of a convex function, \(T = \nabla \varphi\). In one dimension “\(\nabla\varphi\) with \(\varphi\) convex” means “increasing”, so this is precisely the monotone quantile map generalised. Convexity is what replaces the lost total order.



One case with a closed form: Gaussians
Between \(\mathcal{N}(m_1, C_1)\) and \(\mathcal{N}(m_2, C_2)\) in any dimension,
\[
\boxed{\;W_2^2 \;=\; \lVert m_1 - m_2 \rVert^2
\;+\; \operatorname{tr}\!\Big( C_1 + C_2 - 2\big(C_2^{1/2} C_1 C_2^{1/2}\big)^{1/2} \Big).\;}
\]
This is the Bures–Wasserstein distance. When the covariances commute — in particular when both are diagonal — the trace term collapses to \(\lVert C_1^{1/2} - C_2^{1/2} \rVert_F^2\), so the means contribute Euclidean distance and the covariances contribute Frobenius distance between the square roots.
(Checked numerically: for a 2-D pair the formula gives \(2.35331\), and exact optimal transport between \(4{,}000\)-point empirical samples gives \(2.35356\).)
This is the formula behind the Fréchet Inception Distance, which is simply \(W_2\) between two Gaussians fitted to network features — accurate only to the extent that those features really are Gaussian.


The two costs of using it in high dimension
Computation is the visible cost, and it is the one people usually try to fix. Entropic regularisation adds \(\varepsilon H(\gamma)\) to the objective, which makes it strictly convex and solvable by Sinkhorn iterations costing \(O(n^2)\) each — fast and differentiable, at the price of a blurred plan and a biased distance.
Statistics is the cost that actually bites. The empirical Wasserstein distance converges to the truth at rate
\[
\mathbb{E}\,W_p(P_n, P) \;\asymp\; n^{-1/d} \qquad (d > 2p),
\]
which is the curse of dimensionality again, in a new costume. Measured on independent samples from \(\mathcal{N}(0, I_d)\):



\(d\)
fitted slope of \(\log W_2\) against \(\log n\)
\(-1/d\)




5
\(-0.193\)
\(-0.200\)


10
\(-0.106\)
\(-0.100\)


20
\(-0.065\)
\(-0.050\)



So a Wasserstein distance estimated from samples in high dimension is mostly noise, however exactly you solve the transport problem. Solving the wrong problem precisely does not help.
Sliced Wasserstein is the standard dodge: project both distributions onto a random direction \(\theta\), where the closed form applies, and average over directions,
\[
SW_p^p(P,Q) = \int_{\mathbb{S}^{d-1}} W_p^p\big(\theta_\# P,\ \theta_\# Q\big)\, d\theta .
\]
Each slice is a sort. It is a genuine metric, it is cheap, and it inherits the better one-dimensional rate — at the cost of being a weaker comparison that can be fooled by structure invisible to every projection.

title: 07 · Comparing Distributions: From CDFs to KL, and the Two Families
text:
6. Integral probability metrics, in general
Wasserstein and MMD are both instances of one construction. Given a class \(\mathcal{F}\) of real-valued test functions,
\[
d_{\mathcal{F}}(P,Q) \;=\; \sup_{f \in \mathcal{F}}
\Big| \mathbb{E}_{P}[f] - \mathbb{E}_{Q}[f] \Big| .
\]
Read it as a search for a witness: a single function on which the two distributions disagree as loudly as possible. If no test function can tell them apart, they are the same as far as \(\mathcal{F}\) can see.
Everything depends on how rich \(\mathcal{F}\) is, and the choice is a genuine trade-off in both directions:

\(\mathcal{F}\) too small and the metric is blind — it will report zero for distributions that genuinely differ.
\(\mathcal{F}\) too large and the supremum cannot be estimated from finitely many samples — the empirical witness overfits, and the estimate is biased upward no matter how much data you have.









Class \(\mathcal{F}\)
Resulting IPM
Witness is




\(\lVert f \rVert_{\mathrm{Lip}} \le 1\)
Wasserstein-1
a Lipschitz function — the WGAN critic


unit ball of an RKHS \(\mathcal{H}\)
MMD
available in closed form (§7)


\(\lVert f \rVert_\infty \le \tfrac12\)
total variation
an indicator of a set


bounded, with bounded derivatives
Dudley metric
a smooth bump



Two structural remarks. First, IPMs are symmetric and satisfy the triangle inequality whenever \(\mathcal{F}\) is symmetric (\(f \in \mathcal{F} \Rightarrow
-f \in \mathcal{F}\)), so they are honest metrics — unlike KL. Second, and this is the substantive contrast with §4, an IPM is defined through expectations of functions on the space, so it knows how far apart points are. An \(f\)-divergence is defined through a ratio of densities at the same point, so it knows only how much the two disagree there, never how far anything had to move. That single difference is what §8 is about.
Total variation is the intersection. It is an \(f\)-divergence (\(f(t) = \tfrac12|t-1|\)) and an IPM (bounded test functions) and a metric — essentially the only member of both families, which is a good way to remember that they are otherwise disjoint.

title: 07 · Comparing Distributions: From CDFs to KL, and the Two Families
section: 7. Maximum mean discrepancy: the IPM you can actually compute
text:
7. Maximum mean discrepancy: the IPM you can actually compute
Wasserstein’s definition contains an infimum over couplings; the IPM form contains a supremum over functions. Both are optimisation problems. MMD is the choice of \(\mathcal{F}\) for which the optimisation can be solved in closed form, and that is essentially the whole reason it exists.
Take \(\mathcal{F}\) to be the unit ball of a reproducing kernel Hilbert space \(\mathcal{H}\) with kernel \(k\). Define the kernel mean embedding of a distribution,
\[
\mu_P \;=\; \mathbb{E}_{X \sim P}\big[\, k(X, \cdot)\,\big] \;\in\; \mathcal{H},
\]
a single point in \(\mathcal{H}\) that summarises the whole distribution. The reproducing property gives \(\mathbb{E}_P[f] = \langle f, \mu_P\rangle\) for every \(f \in \mathcal{H}\), so
\[
\mathrm{MMD}(P,Q) = \sup_{\lVert f \rVert_{\mathcal{H}} \le 1}
\langle f, \mu_P - \mu_Q \rangle = \lVert \mu_P - \mu_Q \rVert_{\mathcal{H}} .
\]
The supremum is attained by the obvious witness, \(f \propto \mu_P - \mu_Q\), and the value is just a norm. Expanding it,
\[
\boxed{\;\mathrm{MMD}^2(P,Q) = \mathbb{E}\,k(X,X') - 2\,\mathbb{E}\,k(X,Y) + \mathbb{E}\,k(Y,Y')\;}
\]
with \(X, X' \sim P\) and \(Y, Y' \sim Q\) independent. Three expectations of a kernel — no densities, no couplings, no optimisation. Replacing them by sample averages (dropping diagonal terms) gives an unbiased estimator computable in \(O(n^2)\), or \(O(n)\) with a linear-time variant.
Does it separate distributions? Only if the kernel is characteristic, meaning \(P \mapsto \mu_P\) is injective. The Gaussian RBF and Laplace kernels are; a linear kernel is not — it embeds only the mean, so it cannot distinguish any two distributions with the same mean. With a characteristic kernel, \(\mathrm{MMD}(P,Q) = 0 \iff P = Q\).
A closed form to test against. For \(P = \mathcal{N}(a, I_d)\), \(Q = \mathcal{N}(b, I_d)\) and Gaussian kernel of bandwidth \(s\),
\[
\mathrm{MMD}^2 = \frac{2\,s^d}{(2+s^2)^{d/2}}
\left(1 - \exp\!\Big(-\frac{\lVert a-b\rVert^2}{2(2+s^2)}\Big)\right).
\]
(Checked: at \(\lVert a - b\rVert = 1\) and \(s = \sqrt{d}\), the formula gives \(0.1175\), \(0.0328\), \(0.0072\) for \(d = 2, 10, 50\), and the sample estimator returns \(0.1214\), \(0.0317\), \(0.0071\).)

The headline property, and its asterisk
The MMD estimator converges at \(n^{-1/2}\) independently of the dimension — there is no \(n^{-1/d}\) anywhere. Measured slopes of \(\log|\hat{}-\text{truth}|\) against \(\log n\): \(-0.55\) at \(d=2\), \(-0.71\) at \(d=10\), \(-0.48\) at \(d=50\). Against Wasserstein’s \(n^{-1/d}\) this looks like a free lunch.






It is not a free lunch



Look again at the closed form above. For a fixed separation \(\lVert a-b\rVert = 1\), the population MMD itself falls with dimension — \(0.1175\), \(0.0328\), \(0.0072\) at \(d = 2, 10, 50\). The error shrinks at \(n^{-1/2}\) regardless of \(d\), but the signal you are trying to detect shrinks too. What matters for a test is the ratio, and that still degrades.
So the honest statement is: MMD moves the curse from the estimation rate into the effect size. It does not abolish it. It also depends on a bandwidth \(s\) that you must choose — the median heuristic (set \(s\) to the median pairwise distance) is the usual default and is a heuristic, not a theorem.


MMD’s real strengths are that it needs only samples, costs \(O(n^2)\) with no inner optimisation, is differentiable in the samples — hence usable directly as a training loss, as in MMD-GAN — and comes with a clean two-sample test (Gretton et al.), which is how one asks “did my generative model actually match the data?” with a \(p\)-value attached.

section: 8. Why the distinction is not pedantry: disjoint supports
text:
8. Why the distinction is not pedantry: disjoint supports
Take \(P\) uniform on \([0,1]\) and \(Q\) uniform on \([d, d+1]\) — the same shape, shifted by \(d\). Watch what each measure reports as \(d\) grows:

Once the supports separate, every \(f\)-divergence stops responding. KL is already infinite; JS is pinned at \(\log 2\); TV is pinned at 1. They report “as different as possible” and cannot distinguish a near miss from a wild one. Their gradients with respect to \(d\) are zero — so a model trained on them gets no signal telling it which way to move.
\(W_1\) reports \(d\). It keeps growing, and its gradient points home.






This is the WGAN argument



Arjovsky, Chintala and Bottou (2017) built Wasserstein GAN on exactly this observation. A generator’s output distribution is supported on a low-dimensional manifold in a high-dimensional space — the manifold hypothesis of Measuring Things — and so is the data. Two such manifolds generically intersect in a set of measure zero, so the supports are essentially disjoint from the start, and JS (which the original GAN minimises at an optimal discriminator) is pinned at \(\log 2\) with vanishing gradient. Replacing it with \(W_1\), estimated through the Kantorovich–Rubinstein dual with a Lipschitz-constrained critic, restores a usable gradient.
Notice that the same fact motivates diffusion models’ use of noise, for the same reason: convolving with a Gaussian makes the supports overlap, so the ratio-based quantities become finite and informative again.

title: 07 · Comparing Distributions: From CDFs to KL, and the Two Families
section: 9. The map: what is each model family minimising?
text:
9. The map: what is each model family minimising?







Model
Objective, in divergence terms




Maximum likelihood / normalizing flows
forward \(\mathrm{KL}(p_{\text{data}}\|p_\theta)\), exactly (§3)


VAE / autoencoders
maximise the ELBO \(= \log p(x) - \mathrm{KL}(q(z\mid x)\,\|\,p(z\mid x))\); the trainable form contains an explicit \(\mathrm{KL}(q(z\mid x)\,\|\,p(z))\) against the prior


Original GAN
at an optimal discriminator, Jensen–Shannon — an \(f\)-divergence


\(f\)-GAN
any \(f\)-divergence, via its variational (Fenchel) representation


WGAN
\(W_1\) — an IPM, deliberately not an \(f\)-divergence


MMD nets
MMD — also an IPM


Diffusion models
a variational bound that decomposes into a sum of KLs between Gaussians, each with the closed form of §2; equivalently, denoising score matching



Read down that column and the structure the whole field shares comes into view: every generative model is minimising some divergence between the data distribution and the model’s. What distinguishes the families is which divergence, and — because it is usually not computable directly — how they get at it: a bound (VAE), a learned dual (GAN, WGAN), a closed form after adding noise (diffusion), or exactly (flows).






What the next notes do with this



Two rows of that table are now cashed in. Note 08 takes the case where you can write the target down up to a constant and builds a Markov chain that samples it. Note 09 takes the case where you cannot, and shows that training a classifier to separate real from generated samples estimates the density ratio \(p_{\text{data}}/p_g\) — and that the resulting game minimises exactly the Jensen–Shannon divergence in the table above, with §8’s saturation as its central difficulty.








Key takeaway



In one dimension everything is a norm of the CDF gap: sup gives Kolmogorov–Smirnov, \(L^1\) gives Wasserstein-1 which is a transport cost, \(L^2\) gives Cramér–von Mises. Beyond one dimension the CDF fails and two families take over. \(f\)-divergences — KL, JS, TV, \(\chi^2\) — compare densities through their pointwise ratio and are blind to distance, which makes them infinite or saturated when supports disagree. Integral probability metrics — Wasserstein, MMD — compare through test functions and do see distance, which is why they keep working when the supports come apart. Total variation is the one member of both.

Exercises

Show that in one dimension the monotone coupling is optimal for any convex cost, and deduce \(W_1 = \int|F-G|\).
Verify the Bures–Wasserstein formula for two diagonal Gaussians directly, and confirm it reduces to \(\lVert C_1^{1/2}-C_2^{1/2}\rVert_F^2\) plus the squared mean gap.
Why does the quantile construction fail in \(\mathbb{R}^2\)? Give two distributions for which several distinct plans have the same cost.
Brenier’s map is \(\nabla\varphi\) with \(\varphi\) convex. What is \(\varphi\) in one dimension, and why is convexity the right generalisation of monotonicity?
Take \(P=\mathcal{N}(0,I_d)\) and \(Q=\mathcal{N}(\delta e_1, I_d)\). Compute \(W_2\) exactly. Now compute the sliced Wasserstein distance and compare.
Show any IPM with a symmetric \(\mathcal{F}\) obeys the triangle inequality.
Show a linear kernel is not characteristic by exhibiting \(P \ne Q\) with \(\mathrm{MMD}=0\).
Derive the MMD expansion \(\mathbb{E}k(X,X') - 2\mathbb{E}k(X,Y) +
\mathbb{E}k(Y,Y')\) from \(\lVert \mu_P-\mu_Q\rVert^2_{\mathcal{H}}\).
Using the Gaussian-kernel closed form, compute \(\mathrm{MMD}^2\) at \(\lVert a-b\rVert=1\), \(s=\sqrt{d}\), for \(d=2,10,50\). Explain why the dimension-free \(n^{-1/2}\) rate is nevertheless not a free lunch.
Why is the diagonal dropped from the MMD estimator? What happens if you keep it?


Earlier exercises

For \(P = \mathcal{N}(0,1)\) and \(Q = \mathcal{N}(\mu,1)\), show the KS statistic is \(2\Phi(\mu/2)-1\) by finding where the CDF gap is maximised. Evaluate at \(\mu = 1\) and \(\mu = 4\) and comment on the saturation.
Show \(\int|F-G|\,dx = W_1\) for these two Gaussians equals exactly \(|\mu|\), and explain why it does not saturate.
Derive \(\mathrm{KL}(\mathcal{N}(\mu_1,\sigma^2)\|\mathcal{N}(\mu_2,\sigma^2))
= (\mu_1-\mu_2)^2/2\sigma^2\) from the general Gaussian formula, and say why this makes diffusion training objectives reduce to squared errors.
Prove \(\mathrm{KL} \ge 0\) using Jensen, and identify exactly where equality requires \(p = q\) almost everywhere.
Give two distributions with \(\mathrm{KL}(p\|q)\) finite and \(\mathrm{KL}(q\|p) = \infty\). (Hint: make one support strictly contain the other.)
Verify that \(f(t) = t\log t\) gives KL and \(f(t) = \tfrac12|t-1|\) gives total variation in the definition \(D_f = \int q f(p/q)\).
Explain in your own words why no \(f\)-divergence can distinguish “\(Q\) is just beside \(P\)” from “\(Q\) is a mile away”, once the supports are disjoint. Then say what an IPM does differently.
For \(P\) uniform on \([0,1]\) and \(Q\) uniform on \([d,d+1]\) with \(d > 1\), compute \(W_1\), TV and JS. Which of the three would give a usable training gradient in \(d\), and why?

title: 08 · Metropolis–Hastings: Sampling What You Cannot Normalise
text:
1. The problem, stated exactly
Everything this course does is downstream of one request: produce a draw from a distribution. Note 00 argued that generation is sampling; note 06 showed that estimating the density first is hopeless in high dimension. So consider the situation where you are luckier than the image case — you can write down the target, but only up to a constant:
\[
\pi(x) \;=\; \frac{\tilde\pi(x)}{Z}, \qquad Z = \int \tilde\pi(x)\,dx ,
\]
with \(\tilde\pi\) cheap to evaluate at any point and \(Z\) an integral nobody can do.
This is not a contrived setup; it is the generic one.
Bayesian inference. The posterior over parameters given data is
\[
\pi(\theta) \;=\; p(\theta \mid \mathcal{D}) \;=\; \frac{p(\theta)\,L(\mathcal{D}\mid\theta)}{p(\mathcal{D})},
\qquad
p(\mathcal{D}) = \int p(\theta)L(\mathcal{D}\mid\theta)\,d\theta .
\]
The numerator is prior times likelihood — two things you chose and can evaluate in closed form. The denominator, the evidence, is an integral over the whole parameter space, and outside conjugate families it has no closed form and no usable quadrature past a handful of dimensions. So \(\tilde\pi = p(\theta)L\) is available and \(Z = p(\mathcal{D})\) is not.
Energy-based models. \(\pi(x) \propto e^{-E(x)}\) for an energy \(E\) you specify or learn. \(Z = \int e^{-E}\) is the partition function, and computing it is as hard as the original problem.
Conditioning of any kind. \(\pi(x) \propto p(x)\mathbf{1}\{x \in A\}\) — a known distribution restricted to a region. The restricted density is trivial to evaluate and its mass \(p(A)\) is not.

title: 08 · Metropolis–Hastings: Sampling What You Cannot Normalise
text:
What note 06 already settled



Two facts carry over and are not re-derived here.
Rejection sampling is exact and unusable. It needs an envelope \(\pi \le M q\), and in \(d\) dimensions with a proposal only ten percent too wide the acceptance rate is \(1.1^{-d}\) — about \(7\times10^{-5}\) at \(d=100\). Every independently drawn candidate is a fresh gamble against the same odds.
The cure is to stop starting over. Move from where you already are, so that work already done is not thrown away. That is what a Markov chain buys, and what this note builds.

title: 08 · Metropolis–Hastings: Sampling What You Cannot Normalise
text:
2. Chains, kernels, and what “converges” means
A Markov chain on a state space \(\mathcal{X}\) is a sequence \(x_0, x_1, x_2,
\dots\) in which the next state depends on the past only through the present:
\[
\mathbb{P}(x_{t+1} \in A \mid x_t, x_{t-1}, \dots, x_0) \;=\; \mathbb{P}(x_{t+1} \in A \mid x_t)
\;=\; \int_A K(x_t, y)\,dy .
\]
The function \(K(x,y)\) is the transition kernel: the density of where you go next, given where you are. It is all the chain is.
Run the kernel forward from an initial law \(p_0\) and you get a sequence of distributions, not one distribution:
\[
p_{t+1}(y) \;=\; \int p_t(x)\,K(x,y)\,dx .
\]
This is the same \(p_0, p_1, p_2, \dots\) that note 06 exhibited in closed form for Gibbs on a bivariate normal, where \(x_t \mid x_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(\rho^{2t}x_0,\,
1-\rho^{4t})\). Watching that sequence flow is the whole subject.
A distribution \(\pi\) is stationary (or invariant) for \(K\) when applying the kernel changes nothing:
\[
\boxed{\;\pi(y) \;=\; \int \pi(x)\,K(x,y)\,dx.\;}
\]
Stationarity says: if you are already distributed as \(\pi\), one more step leaves you distributed as \(\pi\). It says nothing on its own about getting there. Two more conditions supply that.

Irreducibility: from any starting point the chain can reach any region of positive \(\pi\)-mass. No part of the space is walled off.
Aperiodicity: the chain does not cycle through regions on a fixed schedule.

With those, the fundamental theorem of MCMC applies: the chain is ergodic, \(p_t \to \pi\) regardless of \(p_0\), and time averages converge to space averages,
\[
\frac1T \sum_{t=1}^{T} f(x_t) \;\xrightarrow[T\to\infty]{}\; \mathbb{E}_{\pi}[f(X)] .
\]
That last line is the working promise: run one chain long enough and average along it, and you get expectations under \(\pi\) — even though no single \(x_t\) was drawn from \(\pi\) and no two of them are independent.
So the design problem is now sharp, and it runs backwards from the usual one. Ordinarily you are given a chain and asked for its stationary law. Here you are given the stationary law and asked to build a chain. Metropolis–Hastings is a universal answer.

title: 08 · Metropolis–Hastings: Sampling What You Cannot Normalise
section: 3. Detailed balance: a sufficient condition you can actually check
text:
3. Detailed balance: a sufficient condition you can actually check
Verifying \(\pi = \pi K\) directly means doing an integral over the whole space, which is the sort of thing we are trying to avoid. There is a stronger, purely local condition that implies it. A chain satisfies detailed balance with respect to \(\pi\) if for every pair of states,
\[
\boxed{\;\pi(x)\,K(x,y) \;=\; \pi(y)\,K(y,x).\;}
\]
Read it as a flow statement: at equilibrium the probability mass moving from \(x\) to \(y\) exactly equals the mass moving from \(y\) to \(x\). Every pairwise exchange balances — hence reversible: a film of the chain in equilibrium looks the same run backwards.
Detailed balance implies stationarity. One line:
\[
\int \pi(x)K(x,y)\,dx
\;=\; \int \pi(y)K(y,x)\,dx
\;=\; \pi(y)\int K(y,x)\,dx
\;=\; \pi(y),
\]
using detailed balance in the first step and \(\int K(y,x)dx = 1\) in the last. \(\square\)
The converse is false — plenty of useful chains are stationary without being reversible, and some deliberately non-reversible chains mix faster. But detailed balance is a pointwise condition on two states at a time, which means it can be engineered, and that is exactly what the next section does.
crumbs: 08 · Metropolis–Hastings: Sampling What You Cannot Normalise

title: 08 · Metropolis–Hastings: Sampling What You Cannot Normalise
text:
4. The algorithm
Choose a proposal \(q(y \mid x)\): any conditional distribution you can sample from. It need not resemble \(\pi\); it need not be symmetric; it carries no theoretical burden at all. From the current state \(x_t\):

Propose \(y \sim q(\cdot \mid x_t)\).
Compute the acceptance probability \[
\boxed{\;\alpha(x_t, y) \;=\; \min\!\left\{1,\;
\frac{\pi(y)\,q(x_t \mid y)}{\pi(x_t)\,q(y \mid x_t)}\right\}.\;}
\]
Accept or reject: draw \(u \sim \mathrm{Uniform}(0,1)\); set \(x_{t+1} = y\) if \(u < \alpha\), and otherwise \(x_{t+1} = x_t\) — stay where you are.

Three observations, in order of importance.
The normalising constant cancels. \(\pi\) enters only as the ratio \(\pi(y)/\pi(x)\), and
\[
\frac{\pi(y)}{\pi(x)} \;=\; \frac{\tilde\pi(y)/Z}{\tilde\pi(x)/Z} \;=\; \frac{\tilde\pi(y)}{\tilde\pi(x)} .
\]
\(Z\) never appears. For a Bayesian posterior the rule is literally
\[
\alpha \;=\; \min\left\{1,\; \frac{p(\theta')\,L(\mathcal{D}\mid\theta')}{p(\theta)\,L(\mathcal{D}\mid\theta)}
\cdot \frac{q(\theta \mid \theta')}{q(\theta' \mid \theta)}\right\},
\]
prior times likelihood at two points, and nothing else. The evidence integral — the reason the posterior was intractable — is gone.
Rejection is not a wasted draw. In rejection sampling a rejected candidate disappears and the sampler has nothing to show for it. Here a rejection emits the current state again, which is a genuine sample. Staying put is a legal move, and it is how the chain gives extra weight to high-probability regions. Omitting the repeat — recording only accepted states — is the single most common implementation bug, and it silently biases every estimate.
The correction term \(q(x\mid y)/q(y\mid x)\) is Hastings’ contribution. It compensates for a proposal that is easier to enter a region than to leave it. Metropolis’ original 1953 algorithm assumed a symmetric proposal; Hastings generalised it in 1970 to arbitrary \(q\).

Why it works
Take \(y \ne x\). The MH kernel is \(K(x,y) = q(y\mid x)\,\alpha(x,y)\), so
\[
\pi(x)K(x,y)
= \pi(x)\,q(y\mid x)\,\min\!\left\{1, \frac{\pi(y)q(x\mid y)}{\pi(x)q(y\mid x)}\right\}
= \min\big\{\pi(x)q(y\mid x),\; \pi(y)q(x\mid y)\big\},
\]
pushing the positive factor \(\pi(x)q(y\mid x)\) inside the \(\min\). The right-hand side is symmetric under \(x \leftrightarrow y\) — swapping the labels swaps the two arguments of a \(\min\) and changes nothing. Therefore \(\pi(x)K(x,y) =
\pi(y)K(y,x)\): detailed balance holds, and by §3 so does stationarity. For \(x = y\) the condition is trivial, and the rejection atom is exactly what makes \(K\) integrate to one. \(\square\)
That is the entire theory. The acceptance rule was reverse-engineered to make a \(\min\) appear symmetrically — this is the rare algorithm whose correctness proof is shorter than its motivation.






Where the accept/reject step goes in this course



Metropolis–Hastings needs the accept/reject correction because the proposal is picked for convenience and is therefore wrong. The step is a patch applied to a mismatch.
A diffusion model has no such step. Its reverse process is built so that each small step is already almost exactly right — the forward process adds a tiny bit of Gaussian noise, so the reverse conditional is nearly Gaussian and can be matched directly. There is nothing left to accept or reject.
Keep the contrast in view: MH corrects a bad proposal; a diffusion model learns a good one.

title: 08 · Metropolis–Hastings: Sampling What You Cannot Normalise
section: 5. The three special cases you will meet
text:
5. The three special cases you will meet
Random-walk Metropolis. Take \(q(y\mid x) = \mathcal{N}(y; x, \tau^2 I)\) — a symmetric jump. Then \(q(x\mid y) = q(y\mid x)\), the Hastings ratio is 1, and
\[
\alpha \;=\; \min\left\{1, \frac{\pi(y)}{\pi(x)}\right\}.
\]
Always move uphill; move downhill with probability equal to the density ratio. That downhill move is not a defect — it is precisely what separates sampling from optimisation. A hill-climber ends at the mode and reports one point; a sampler must visit the tails in proportion to their mass, so it has to be willing to go down.
The independence sampler. \(q(y \mid x) = q(y)\), ignoring the current state. Then \(\alpha = \min\{1, w(y)/w(x)\}\) with importance weight \(w = \pi/q\): accept whenever the candidate has a better weight than the incumbent. This is rejection sampling’s cousin and inherits its fragility — a proposal with lighter tails than \(\pi\) makes the chain stick for astronomically long stretches.
Gibbs sampling is MH with \(\alpha \equiv 1\). Propose by redrawing one coordinate from its exact conditional, \(q(y_i \mid x) = \pi(y_i \mid x_{-i})\), leaving the others fixed. Substituting into the acceptance ratio and using \(\pi(x) = \pi(x_i \mid x_{-i})\pi(x_{-i})\), everything cancels and \(\alpha = 1\). Gibbs never rejects — the price is that you must be able to sample each conditional exactly, which is a strong requirement.






MALA: the score walks in



Nothing forces the proposal to be blind. Metropolis-adjusted Langevin proposes
\[
y \;=\; x + \tfrac{\tau^2}{2}\,\nabla_x \log \pi(x) + \tau\,z, \qquad z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I),
\]
then applies the usual accept/reject step (the proposal is now asymmetric, so the Hastings ratio matters). The drift term pushes candidates toward high density before they are judged, so acceptance stays high with much larger steps.
And notice what it needs: only \(\nabla_x \log \pi\), the score. The normalising constant differentiates away, exactly as in note 06. Drop the accept/reject step and you have unadjusted Langevin dynamics — biased by \(O(\tau)\), but needing nothing except the score.
This is the closest classical ancestor of a score-based generative model. Module 4 will learn \(\nabla_x\log p\) from data instead of deriving it; the sampler on top is this one.

title: 08 · Metropolis–Hastings: Sampling What You Cannot Normalise
section: 6. A worked example: two lines of arithmetic
text:
6. A worked example: two lines of arithmetic
Target: the posterior for a Gaussian mean with a Gaussian prior,
\[
\theta \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 10^2), \qquad
x_1,\dots,x_n \mid \theta \sim \mathcal{N}(\theta, 1),
\]
so that \(\tilde\pi(\theta) = \exp\!\big(-\tfrac{\theta^2}{200}\big)\cdot
\exp\!\big(-\tfrac12\sum_i (x_i-\theta)^2\big)\). Work on the log scale — always work on the log scale, or the products underflow to zero by \(n \approx 500\):
\[
\log\alpha \;=\; \min\Big\{0,\;\; \log\tilde\pi(\theta') - \log\tilde\pi(\theta)\Big\},
\]
with \(\log\tilde\pi(\theta) = -\tfrac{\theta^2}{200} - \tfrac12\sum_i(x_i-\theta)^2\). Propose \(\theta' = \theta + \tau z\), accept if \(\log u < \log\alpha\).
This example is conjugate, so the answer is known — \(\mathcal{N}\!\big(\frac{n\bar x}{n + 1/100},\, \frac{1}{n+1/100}\big)\) — which is the point: run the sampler, overlay the histogram on the exact posterior, and confirm that a procedure using only ratios of unnormalised densities reproduces a distribution whose normalising constant it never computed. Then change the prior to a Student-\(t\), destroy conjugacy, and observe that the code does not change at all. That robustness is why MH dominated applied Bayesian statistics for thirty years.

title: 08 · Metropolis–Hastings: Sampling What You Cannot Normalise
section: 7. What it costs: burn-in, correlation, and tuning
text:
7. What it costs: burn-in, correlation, and tuning
The theorem says \(p_t \to \pi\). It does not say when, and everything difficult about MCMC lives in that gap.
Burn-in. The chain starts at \(p_0\), which is wherever you put it, and needs time before \(p_t\) resembles \(\pi\). Early samples are discarded. How many is a judgement call, informed by trace plots and by running several chains from dispersed starts and checking they agree (the Gelman–Rubin \(\hat R\) statistic, which compares between-chain to within-chain variance and should approach 1).
Autocorrelation. Consecutive states are dependent by construction. \(T\) MCMC draws are worth fewer than \(T\) independent ones — the effective sample size is
\[
\mathrm{ESS} \;=\; \frac{T}{1 + 2\sum_{k\ge1}\rho_k},
\]
with \(\rho_k\) the lag-\(k\) autocorrelation. Note 06’s Gibbs example makes this concrete: lag-1 autocorrelation \(\rho^2\), so a target with correlation \(0.99\) gives \(\rho^2 \approx 0.98\) and an ESS a fiftieth of the chain length. Strongly dependent targets are expensive.
Step size is a genuine dilemma. For random-walk Metropolis with scale \(\tau\):








\(\tau\)
acceptance

too small
\(\to 1\)
almost every move accepted, but each is tiny — the chain diffuses, needing \(\sim(L/\tau)^2\) steps to cross a region of width \(L\)

\(\to 0\)
proposals land in the tails and are rejected; the chain sticks at one point for hundreds of iterations

\(\approx 0.234\)

A first-time user’s instinct — “high acceptance means it is working” — is exactly backwards. An acceptance rate of \(0.95\) almost always means the chain is crawling.
Multimodality is the failure MCMC hides best. A chain in one mode of a well-separated bimodal target must cross a low-density valley to reach the other, and the probability of proposing across it can be \(e^{-100}\). The chain then looks perfectly healthy — good acceptance, stable trace, tight autocorrelation — while sampling from the wrong distribution. It has converged to a mode, not to \(\pi\). Tempering, parallel chains and mode-hopping proposals exist; none is a general solution.






And the curse, once more



Even with none of the above going wrong, the number of steps needed to produce one effectively independent sample grows with dimension. For product-form targets the standard scaling results are



sampler
steps per independent sample




random-walk Metropolis
\(O(d)\)


MALA (Langevin, adjusted)

Each row is a real improvement, bought with more gradient information per step — and every row still grows. Compare rejection sampling’s \(\sigma^{-d}\) and this is a triumph: polynomial instead of exponential. Compare it with the \(d \approx
10^5\) of a modest image and it is still nowhere near enough.

title: 08 · Metropolis–Hastings: Sampling What You Cannot Normalise
section: 8. The structural reason this is not a generative model
text:
8. The structural reason this is not a generative model
Suppose every difficulty in §7 were solved: a perfectly tuned sampler, no multimodality, dimension-free mixing. It would still not generate an image. The obstruction is not efficiency. It is the input.
Metropolis–Hastings requires \(\tilde\pi\): a function you can evaluate at any proposed point. It answers

“I can write down the target up to a constant. Give me samples.”

Generative modelling asks the opposite question:

“I cannot write down the target at all. I have 60,000 samples from it. Give me more.”

There is no \(\tilde\pi(x)\) for natural images. Nobody can supply a function that, given a \(256\times256\times3\) array, returns a number proportional to how likely that array is to be a photograph. That function is precisely the thing note 06 proved we cannot estimate. MH is a machine for converting a density into samples, and we have no density to feed it.
Notice too that MH never learns. Run it for a million steps, then ask for a sample from a fresh start and you pay the full burn-in again. There is no trained object, nothing amortised, no reuse. A generative model, by contrast, pays a large training cost once and then produces a sample in a single forward pass.






The pivot the lecture turns on



Note 06 already named the shape of the fix. In rejection sampling, in MH, in Gibbs, a human picks the proposal for convenience and hopes it resembles the target — and in high dimension it does not.
So stop picking it. Learn it. Learn a map \(G\) from easy noise to data, fit it using only samples, and dispense with the density entirely.
That immediately raises the question that defines the next note: if you never evaluate a density, how do you know your generator is any good? You cannot compute a likelihood, so you cannot maximise one. The answer — train a second network to tell your samples from real ones, and improve until it cannot — is the generative adversarial network, and it is the subject of note 09.
