title: Joint, Marginal, Conditional — and Bayes
text:
1. Two colorings, one blob
Recall the picture: a blob \(\Omega\) of unit mass, a probability measure \(P\) weighing its regions, and a random variable as numbers painted on the blob. Now paint the blob twice: two measurable functions
\[
X : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad Y : \Omega \to \mathbb{R},
\]
on the same blob. This co-residence is the whole point. “\(X\) and \(Y\) are jointly distributed” is not an extra assumption bolted on later; it is the statement that one outcome \(\omega\) determines both numbers at once — height and weight of the same person, today’s price and tomorrow’s price of the same stock, clean image and noisy image from the same generation run.
The pair is a single map into the plane,
\[
(X, Y) : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}^2,
\qquad
\mu_{X,Y} \;=\; (X,Y)_\# P,
\]
and the pushforward \(\mu_{X,Y}\) — the blob’s mass transported to the plane — is the joint distribution. When it has a density \(p(x,y)\), picture the joint as a mountain of mass over the plane: total volume \(1\), height = mass per unit area.

title: Joint, Marginal, Conditional — and Bayes
section: 2. Marginals are shadows — and shadows forget
text:
2. Marginals are shadows — and shadows forget
The marginal of \(X\) is nothing new: it is the pushforward of \(P\) under \(X\) alone, obtained from the joint by integrating out the other coordinate,
\[
p(x) = \int p(x, y)\, dy ,
\qquad
p(y) = \int p(x, y)\, dx .
\]
Geometrically: collapse the mountain onto one axis — the marginal is the mountain’s shadow. And a shadow forgets. It records how much mass sits over each \(x\), but nothing about how that mass is distributed in \(y\).
This forgetting is a one-way street with a name you will meet again:






Key takeaway: many mountains, same shadows



The map from joints to marginal pairs is many-to-one. Fix both shadows to be standard normal; then every correlation \(\rho \in (-1, 1)\) gives a different mountain casting those same two shadows (Act I of the demo below — drag \(\rho\) and watch the mountain twist while the shadows stand still). Those are only the jointly Gaussian couplings of two standard normals; that pair admits many non-Gaussian couplings too.
Twisting one ellipse is the mild version of the point. Here is the version you cannot argue with. Write \(N_{(u,v)}(x,y) = \mathcal{N}(x; u, s^2)\,
\mathcal{N}(y; v, s^2)\) for a round Gaussian lump of width \(s\) centred at \((u,v)\), fix \(a > s > 0\), and put lumps at the four corners \((\pm a, \pm a)\). Build three joints by placing mass on them differently:
\[
\begin{aligned}
p_{\nearrow}(x,y) &= \tfrac12 N_{(-a,-a)} + \tfrac12 N_{(+a,+a)}, \\
p_{\searrow}(x,y) &= \tfrac12 N_{(-a,+a)} + \tfrac12 N_{(+a,-a)}, \\
p_{\boxplus}(x,y) &= \tfrac14 \big( N_{(-a,-a)} + N_{(+a,+a)} + N_{(-a,+a)} + N_{(+a,-a)} \big).
\end{aligned}
\]
Integrating \(N_{(u,v)}\) over \(y\) leaves exactly \(\mathcal{N}(x; u, s^2)\), so each joint’s \(x\)-marginal is the weighted sum of its lumps’ \(x\)-factors. In every one of the three, the total weight sitting at \(u = -a\) is \(\tfrac12\) and at \(u = +a\) is \(\tfrac12\) — and likewise in \(y\). So all three have the identical pair of shadows, exactly and not approximately: the same two-bump curve
\[
p(x) \;=\; \tfrac12\, \mathcal{N}(x; -a, s^2) + \tfrac12\, \mathcal{N}(x; +a, s^2)
\]
on each axis. Yet one is two lumps on the rising diagonal, one is two lumps on the falling diagonal, and one is four lumps in a square. Their correlations are \(+\tfrac{a^2}{a^2 + s^2}\), \(-\tfrac{a^2}{a^2 + s^2}\) and \(0\) — strongly positive, strongly negative, and exactly zero (using \(\operatorname{Var}(X) = a^2 + s^2\)). The third is genuinely independent — it is the product of its marginals. The first two are dependent, with correlation magnitude approaching \(1\) as \(a/s\) grows.
Click through the three in Act I of the demo and watch the shadow curves on the edges: they do not so much as flicker. Nothing computed from the marginals alone — not their means, not their variances, not their complete one-dimensional shapes — distinguishes joints this different. And note where the correlation sits in this: it is not computable from the marginals either. It is joint information, one number’s worth, which the shadows have thrown away along with everything else. A joint with prescribed marginals is called a coupling of them, and the set of couplings is enormous. Many generative constructions induce a coupling of noise and data — a particular mountain over the (noise, data) plane — and some, such as minibatch-OT flow matching, select one on purpose. The transport tutorials (the intuitive story and the rigorous account) study what additional structure picks out a map, a coupling, a kernel or a path; tutorial 10 is insistent that merely exhibiting a coupling explains less than it appears to. The mathematics of that choice starts here, with the fact that shadows do not determine the mountain.


One special coupling deserves its name now: \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent when the joint is the product of the marginals, \(p(x,y) = p(x)\,p(y)\) — the mountain built by extruding one shadow along the other, with no interaction. Independence is thus one point in the vast space of couplings, not the typical case; elementary courses over-expose it because it is the easiest mountain to compute with.
Interactive demo — The Joint Slicer

title: Joint, Marginal, Conditional — and Bayes
text:
3. Conditionals are slices, renormalized
Fix a value \(x_0\) and ask: given that \(X = x_0\), how is \(Y\) distributed? On the mountain, the answer is geometric: cut a vertical slice through the mountain at \(x = x_0\). The slice’s profile \(y \mapsto p(x_0, y)\) has the right shape but the wrong total — it is a sliver of mass, not a probability distribution. So renormalize: divide by the slice’s own area, which is exactly the marginal \(p(x_0)\). The result is the conditional density
\[
p(y \mid x_0) \;=\; \frac{p(x_0, y)}{p(x_0)} .
\]
Slice, then renormalize. That is the entire definition, and Act I of the demo lets you drag the slice line and watch both steps: the raw sliver (dashed) and its re-inflated version (solid).
In blob language, for an event \(B\) with \(P(B) > 0\), conditioning genuinely does restrict the blob to \(B\) and rescale: \(P(A \mid B) = P(A \cap B)/P(B)\), ordinary division.
For \(X = x_0\) with a continuous \(X\) that story is not available, and it is worth being exact about why. The fibre \(\{X = x_0\}\) has mass zero; there is nothing to rescale, and \(0/0\) is not a definition. So the displayed formula is not restriction-and-rescaling in disguise — it is a new object, and it comes with hypotheses. Assume the joint has a density that is continuous near \(x_0\) and that \(p(x_0) > 0\). Then the quotient defines a natural continuous version of the conditional density, and it is recovered as the limit of thickened slices \(\{x_0 \le X \le x_0 + \varepsilon\}\) as \(\varepsilon \to 0\).
Two caveats to file away. The function \(y \mapsto p(x_0, y)\) is a density cross-section, not a sliver of mass: its integral is the marginal density \(p(x_0)\), not the probability of a zero-width strip. And in general — without the continuity assumption — a conditional law is a disintegration, pinned down only for \(P_X\)-almost every \(x_0\), so different versions may disagree at any particular value.






A lean caution: conditioning on probability-zero events (Borel–Kolmogorov)



Because that limit is taken along shrinking bands, the answer can depend on the shape of the bands. The same probability-zero set can be presented in two ways — say, as the vertical line \(\{X = 0\}\) or as a diagonal-parameterized family that happens to collapse onto that same line — and the two shrinking procedures can yield different conditional distributions. This is the Borel–Kolmogorov paradox. The first half of the rule is simple: a conditional distribution is defined relative to a chosen slicing variable (formally: a chosen \(\sigma\)-algebra), never relative to the bare event. Always know which variable you are conditioning on.
But naming the variable is not quite enough either, and it would be dishonest to stop there. Conditioning on \(\sigma(X)\) determines the conditional law only for \(P_X\)-almost every value; at any single null value \(x_0\) a regular conditional kernel may be redefined at will. So what actually keeps this course safe is not that the slicing variable is explicit — though it always is — but that Gaussian smoothing gives every \(p(x_t \mid x_0)\) and \(p_t\) a positive, smooth density. That supplies a canonical continuous version, and identities between conditionals should otherwise be read as holding almost everywhere.

title: Joint, Marginal, Conditional — and Bayes
section: 4. Bayes’ rule is the freedom to slice both ways
text:
4. Bayes’ rule is the freedom to slice both ways
The mountain does not care which axis you slice along. Vertical slices give \(p(y \mid x)\); horizontal slices give \(p(x \mid y)\); and both factorizations rebuild the same mountain:
\[
p(x, y) \;=\; p(y \mid x)\, p(x) \;=\; p(x \mid y)\, p(y).
\]
Read the second equality as a statement about one object — ribbons of conditional mass, weighted by the shadow, tile the mountain, in either direction — and division gives
\[
p(x \mid y) \;=\; \frac{p(y \mid x)\, p(x)}{p(y)} ,
\qquad
p(y) = \int p(y \mid x)\, p(x)\, dx .
\]
That is Bayes’ rule. On the measure-theoretic picture it is not a new axiom, not a philosophy, not even a theorem of any depth: it is the observation that a mountain admits two slicings. All of its power in applications comes from an asymmetry of availability, not of mathematics — models are naturally specified in one direction (a cause \(x\) producing an observation \(y\) via \(p(y \mid x)\)), while inference needs the other (\(p(x \mid y)\)). Bayes’ rule is the pivot between them.

title: Joint, Marginal, Conditional — and Bayes
text:
5. Mixed joints: the two-shelf picture
Diffusion models constantly condition between a discrete variable and a continuous one, and there the mountain picture needs one adjustment. Let \(z \in
\{-1, +1\}\) be a latent label with \(P(z = -1) = \pi\), and let \(x \mid z \sim
\mathcal{N}(z, \sigma^2)\). The joint of \((z, x)\) is not a mountain over the plane: it is two shelves of 1-D density, one per value of \(z\), holding masses \(\pi\) and \(1 - \pi\):
\[
p(z, x) \;=\;
\begin{cases}
\pi \cdot \mathcal{N}(x; -1, \sigma^2) & z = -1,\\[2pt]
(1-\pi) \cdot \mathcal{N}(x; +1, \sigma^2) & z = +1.
\end{cases}
\]



A mixed joint: one discrete and one continuous variable. The joint is two weighted shelves of density; a vertical slice crosses both shelves, and renormalizing the two heights gives the posterior over z.


Everything from §§2–4 transfers verbatim, with one integral replaced by a sum:

Marginal of \(x\) (shadow of both shelves): the mixture \(p(x) = \pi\, \mathcal{N}(x; -1, \sigma^2) + (1-\pi)\, \mathcal{N}(x; +1,
\sigma^2)\).
Conditional of \(x\) given \(z\) (one shelf, renormalized): just \(\mathcal{N}(x; z, \sigma^2)\) — the model as specified.
Conditional of \(z\) given \(x\) — slice vertically at \(x\). The slice meets two points of mass, the heights of the two shelves; renormalizing the pair gives the posterior

\[
P(z = +1 \mid x)
= \frac{(1-\pi)\, \mathcal{N}(x; +1, \sigma^2)}
       {\pi\, \mathcal{N}(x; -1, \sigma^2) + (1-\pi)\, \mathcal{N}(x; +1, \sigma^2)} .
\]
This is Bayes’ rule again, but now the slice-and-renormalize is a two-bar histogram — Act II of the demo, where the slice line drags across both shelves and the posterior bars re-balance live.

The worked example this course runs on
Set \(\pi = \tfrac12\). Cancel the common factor and simplify the ratio of Gaussians:
\[
P(z = +1 \mid x)
= \frac{\exp\!\big(\!-\tfrac{(x-1)^2}{2\sigma^2}\big)}
       {\exp\!\big(\!-\tfrac{(x+1)^2}{2\sigma^2}\big) + \exp\!\big(\!-\tfrac{(x-1)^2}{2\sigma^2}\big)}
= \frac{1}{1 + e^{-2x/\sigma^2}}
= \operatorname{sigmoid}\!\left(\frac{2x}{\sigma^2}\right),
\]
and therefore the posterior mean of the label is
\[
\mathbb{E}[z \mid x]
= (+1)\,P(z{=}{+1} \mid x) + (-1)\,P(z{=}{-1} \mid x)
= \tanh\!\left(\frac{x}{\sigma^2}\right).
\]
This sigmoid/tanh pair is the exact object that appears in Two-Point Diffusion as the optimal denoiser \(\mathbb{E}[x_0 \mid x]\) — under the dictionary \(z \leftrightarrow x_0\) and \(x \leftrightarrow x_\sigma\), since \(x = z + \sigma\varepsilon\) here is that tutorial’s VE corruption \(x_\sigma = x_0 + \sigma\varepsilon\). (Mind the letter: \(z\) is the clean label here and the noise there.) Concretely: what a denoiser computes is a posterior mean — a slice through a joint of (clean, noisy), renormalized, then averaged. Seen from this tutorial, the W01 formula is one drag of the slice line in Act II.






Key takeaway



Four pictures, one object. The joint is the complete description (mountain, or shelves). Marginals are its shadows — lossy, with many joints per shadow-pair. Conditionals are its slices, renormalized to unit mass — well-defined once you say which variable slices. Bayes’ rule is the identity between the two ways of slicing. Every probabilistic statement in this course — \(p(x_t \mid x_0)\), the posterior over components, \(\mathbb{E}[x_0 \mid x_t]\) — is one of these four moves on some joint.

title: Joint, Marginal, Conditional — and Bayes
text:
6. What is deferred, deliberately
Three objects belong to this storyline but deserve their own installment: likelihood (the conditional read as a function of the parameter, not the data), the score (the gradient of a log-density, i.e. of a log-slice), and KL divergence (a measure-theoretic comparison of two mountains). Where each is actually picked up: likelihood in Distributions and Maximum Likelihood, and the score in Two-Point Diffusion and the probability-flow ODE. KL has no measure-theoretic treatment in the present sequence — it is used in lecture in its working form, and a proper installment is still owed.

title: Joint, Marginal, Conditional — and Bayes
text:
Exercises

Two fair coin tosses; \(X\) = first toss, \(Y\) = number of heads. Write the four nonzero entries of the joint as a \(2 \times 3\) table, compute both marginals (shadow along each axis), and both conditional families. Verify Bayes’ rule on \(P(X = H \mid Y = 1)\).
The standard bivariate normal with correlation \(|\rho| < 1\) has density \[
p(x,y) = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{1-\rho^2}}
  \exp\!\Big(\!-\tfrac{x^2 - 2\rho x y + y^2}{2(1-\rho^2)}\Big).
\] Verify by completing the square in \(y\) that the vertical slice at \(x_0\), renormalized, is \(\mathcal{N}(\rho x_0,\, 1 - \rho^2)\). Confirm both readings against the demo: the slice’s centre moves with \(x_0\) (unless \(\rho = 0\)), while its width is the same for every \(x_0\).
Construct two different joints on \(\{0,1\}^2\) with both marginals uniform. (You have found two couplings of the same shadows. How many are there?)
Show that if \(p(x,y) = p(x)\,p(y)\) then every vertical slice, renormalized, is the same distribution \(p(y)\) — independence means the slices don’t move. Check this in Act I at \(\rho = 0\). Note carefully why that check is legitimate here: the family is jointly Gaussian, and for jointly Gaussian pairs zero correlation does imply independence. In general it does not — the four-lump joint above is uncorrelated and dependent.
Derive the sigmoid posterior above, keeping general \(\pi \in (0,1)\); show the effect of \(\pi \neq \tfrac12\) is an additive shift \(\tfrac{\sigma^2}{2}\log
\tfrac{1-\pi}{\pi}\) in \(x\). Watch the bars in Act II shift as you drag \(\pi\).
For general \(\pi\) the posterior mean is the shifted tanh of Exercise 5, \[
\mathbb{E}[z \mid x] = \tanh\!\Big(\tfrac{x}{\sigma^2}
  + \tfrac12 \log \tfrac{1-\pi}{\pi}\Big),
\] which reduces to \(\tanh(x/\sigma^2)\) only at \(\pi = \tfrac12\). Integrating that against the mixture marginal gives \(\mathbb{E}[\,\mathbb{E}[z \mid x]\,]\) — and you should be able to name the answer, \(1 - 2\pi\), without computing any integral. (This is the tower property; it will become the workhorse identity of the course. Check what goes wrong if you integrate the unshifted \(\tanh(x/\sigma^2)\) against an unequal mixture.)
(Borel–Kolmogorov, lean.) On the unit square with uniform mass, the event “\(Y = X\)” has probability zero. Two different variables vanish exactly on it: \[
U = Y - X, \qquad V = \frac{Y - X}{1 + X}.
\] Both band families \(\{|U| \le \varepsilon\}\) and \(\{|V| \le \varepsilon\} = \{|Y - X| \le \varepsilon(1+X)\}\) shrink to the same diagonal. Parameterising that diagonal by \(x \in [0,1]\), show the first induces the uniform limiting density \(1\) and the second induces \(\tfrac{2(1+x)}{3}\). Same limiting set, different answers — so it is the variable, not the event, that the conditional depends on.

title: Why the Gaussian? Four Arguments for One Density
text:
1. The gap Chebyshev leaves open
Start where the Foundations tutorial stopped. Chebyshev says that for any law with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\),
\[
\mathbb{P}\big(|X - \mu| \ge k\sigma\big) \le \frac{1}{k^{2}} .
\]
It is a genuine theorem and it is tight — some distribution attains it for each \(k\). But look at what it costs to be that general:
Chebyshev’s tail decays polynomially, like \(k^{-2}\). The Gaussian’s decays like \(e^{-k^2/2}\) — not merely faster, but in a different regime altogether. By \(k=4\) the bound is a thousand times too pessimistic.
So the honest question is not “why is the Gaussian’s tail small” but: what extra assumption, beyond a finite variance, buys you \(e^{-k^2/2}\) instead of \(k^{-2}\)? Chebyshev is what you can say knowing two moments and nothing else. Each of the arguments below adds one structural demand — symmetry, or additivity, or ignorance — and each time the answer that comes back is \(e^{-x^2/2}\).
crumbs: Why the Gaussian? Four Arguments for One Density

title: Why the Gaussian? Four Arguments for One Density
crumbs: Why the Gaussian? Four Arguments for One Density

title: Why the Gaussian? Four Arguments for One Density
section: 2. Symmetry plus independence, and the density falls out
text:
2. Symmetry plus independence, and the density falls out
This is the argument that lets you see the density rather than be handed it. It is due to Herschel (1850) and Maxwell (1860), who each wanted the distribution of errors in two dimensions.
Impose exactly two demands on a density \(f\) on \(\mathbb{R}^2\):

The coordinates are independent — \(f(x,y) = g(x)\,g(y)\) for some one-dimensional \(g\), the same in each coordinate.
The density is rotationally symmetric — \(f(x,y)\) depends on \((x,y)\) only through the radius \(\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\). Errors have no preferred direction.

Both are natural for a measurement error: the horizontal and vertical components of a miss should not influence each other, and no direction on the target should be special. Now watch what they force together.
Write the second demand as \(f(x,y) = h(x^2+y^2)\). Combining with the first,
\[
g(x)\,g(y) = h(x^2 + y^2).
\]
Set \(y = 0\): \(g(x)g(0) = h(x^2)\), so \(h(u) = g(\sqrt{u})\,g(0)\). Substituting back,
\[
g(x)\,g(y) \;=\; g\big(\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\big)\,g(0).
\]
Define \(\varphi(u) = g(\sqrt{u})/g(0)\) for \(u \ge 0\). The relation becomes
\[
\varphi(u)\,\varphi(v) \;=\; \varphi(u+v),
\]
which is Cauchy’s exponential functional equation. Its only measurable solutions are \(\varphi(u) = e^{cu}\). Therefore
\[
g(t) \;=\; g(0)\,e^{c t^{2}},
\]
and for \(g\) to be integrable we need \(c < 0\). Write \(c = -1/(2\sigma^2)\) and normalise:
\[
\boxed{\;g(t) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma}\,e^{-t^{2}/2\sigma^{2}}.\;}
\]
The Gaussian, with no probabilistic input at all — only “independent coordinates” and “no preferred direction”, plus the requirement that the answer be a density.






What that argument really shows



The exponent is quadratic because the only rotation-invariant quantity built from independent coordinates is the sum of squares, and the only way to turn a sum into a product is to exponentiate. That is the whole mechanism: \(e^{-\frac12\sum x_i^2} = \prod e^{-x_i^2/2}\). Read it in reverse and it is exactly §2 of the multivariate reference: \(\mathcal{N}(0,I)\) factorises into independent coordinates because its exponent is a sum of squares.
It also explains the shape of the level sets. Rotational symmetry gives circles; apply a linear map and circles become ellipses, which is why every multivariate Gaussian contour is an ellipsoid and no other shape ever appears.
The Gaussian is the only density with independent coordinates and rotational symmetry. Try \(e^{-|t|}\): the product \(e^{-|x|}e^{-|y|} = e^{-(|x|+|y|)}\) has diamond-shaped level sets, not circles. It fails, and so does everything else.
crumbs: Why the Gaussian? Four Arguments for One Density

title: Why the Gaussian? Four Arguments for One Density
section: 3. Maximum entropy: the least committed choice
text:
3. Maximum entropy: the least committed choice
A second demand, of a completely different kind. Suppose all you are willing to assert about a quantity is its mean and its variance. Among all densities with those two moments, which should you pick?
The principled answer is: the one that assumes the least — that is, the one of maximum entropy, \(h(p) = -\int p \log p\). Committing to anything with lower entropy means smuggling in structure you have no evidence for.
The answer is the Gaussian. Let \(q = \mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)\) and let \(p\) be any density with the same mean and variance. Then
\[
0 \;\le\; \mathrm{KL}(p \,\|\, q) \;=\; \int p \log \frac{p}{q}
\;=\; -h(p) - \int p \log q ,
\]
using \(\mathrm{KL} \ge 0\), which is Jensen from the inequalities tutorial. Now the second term: because \(\log q\) is a quadratic in \(x\), the integral \(\int p \log q\) depends on \(p\) only through its mean and variance — which are the same as \(q\)’s by assumption. So \(\int p\log q = \int q \log q = -h(q)\), and the display rearranges to
\[
h(p) \;\le\; h(q),
\]
with equality exactly when \(p = q\). \(\square\)
The step that makes it work is worth naming: \(\log\) of a Gaussian is a quadratic, and a quadratic only sees two moments. Fix a different pair of constraints and you get a different maximum-entropy family — fix the mean alone on \([0,\infty)\) and you get the exponential; fix nothing but a bounded range and you get the uniform. The Gaussian is the maximum-entropy answer to precisely the question “I know the mean and the variance”.
Numerically, at variance \(1\): Gaussian \(h = 1.4189\) nats, Laplace \(1.3466\), uniform \(1.2425\) — the Gaussian wins, as it must.
crumbs: Why the Gaussian? Four Arguments for One Density

title: Why the Gaussian? Four Arguments for One Density
text:
4. The central limit theorem: additivity
The third demand is additivity. Let \(X_1, X_2, \dots\) be i.i.d. with mean \(\mu\) and finite variance \(\sigma^2\) — no other assumption about their distribution. Then
\[
\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{n}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(X_i - \mu)
\;\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{d}\;
\mathcal{N}(0,1).
\]
The weak law of §6 of the inequalities tutorial said the average concentrates on \(\mu\). The CLT says what the residual fluctuation looks like once you magnify it by the right amount: divide by \(n\) and everything collapses to a point; divide by \(\sqrt{n}\) and a fixed shape survives — and that shape is the Gaussian, whatever you started from.
Act III of the Gaussian Lab makes the convergence visible, and also makes visible that the rate depends heavily on the source: a symmetric one like the uniform is close by \(n=3\), while a lopsided exponential or a two-valued coin flip takes far longer. The limit is identical; only the approach differs.
Why this is an argument for the Gaussian and not merely a fact about sums. Measurement error is typically the accumulation of many small independent perturbations. So is thermal noise, and so is the pixel noise in a sensor. If a quantity is a sum of many small independent contributions and you know nothing about the individual terms, the CLT says you already know the shape of the total. That is why Gaussian noise models are so often right without anyone having checked.
And it explains stability. The Gaussian is a fixed point of adding: sum two independent Gaussians and you get a Gaussian, with variances adding. It is the only distribution with finite variance that is stable in this sense, which is why it is the limit — anything else would be changed by the very operation the limit is built from.
crumbs: Why the Gaussian? Four Arguments for One Density

title: Why the Gaussian? Four Arguments for One Density
text:
5. Four demands, one density








Demand
Argument
What forces the exponent




Only two moments known
Chebyshev (§1)
nothing — this is the weak baseline the others improve on


Independent coordinates, no preferred direction
Herschel–Maxwell (§2)
sum of squares is the only rotation-invariant form


Assume as little as possible given mean and variance
maximum entropy (§3)
\(\log\)-Gaussian is quadratic, so it only sees two moments


Sum of many small independent effects
central limit theorem (§4)
stability under addition



Four different starting points — a symmetry, an epistemic principle, a limit theorem — and one density at the end of each. That convergence is what earns the Gaussian its place. It is not that it is convenient, though it is; it is that several quite different demands each single it out uniquely.






Why this course adds Gaussian noise



Every argument above is also a reason the forward process of a diffusion model uses \(\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2 I)\) rather than anything else. It is isotropic, so no direction of image space is privileged (§2). It is the least committed choice given a noise scale (§3). It is stable under composition, so many small steps equal one big step with variances added (§4) — which is what makes \(p(x_t \mid x_0)\) available in closed form at every \(t\) instead of only step-by-step. And it is closed under the linear maps the model applies, per the multivariate reference.
Choose any other noise and all four properties fail at once.
crumbs: Why the Gaussian? Four Arguments for One Density

title: Why the Gaussian? Four Arguments for One Density
text:
Exercises

Complete the Herschel–Maxwell derivation carefully. Where exactly is measurability (or continuity) of \(\varphi\) used, and what goes wrong without it? (Cauchy’s equation has pathological non-measurable solutions.)
Show that \(e^{-|x|}e^{-|y|}\) is not rotationally symmetric by finding two points at the same radius with different densities. Sketch its level sets.
Carry the Herschel–Maxwell argument into \(d\) dimensions and show it yields \(\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2 I_d)\). Which of the two demands does a non-isotropic Gaussian \(\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma)\) violate?
Verify the maximum-entropy proof’s key step: show explicitly that \(\int p \log q\) depends on \(p\) only through \(\int x\,p\) and \(\int x^2 p\) when \(q\) is Gaussian.
Find the maximum-entropy density on \([0,\infty)\) subject to a fixed mean. (Answer: exponential. The same Lagrangian argument, with a different constraint.)
Compute the Chebyshev bound and the true Gaussian tail at \(k = 6\). How large is the discrepancy, and which of §§2–4 explains why the true tail is so much thinner?
(Stability.) Show directly, using the MGF from the multivariate reference, that a sum of two independent Gaussians is Gaussian with variances adding. Then explain why this makes the Gaussian a natural candidate for the CLT limit.

title: The Probability-Flow ODE
The Probability-Flow ODE
text: A diffusion model learns a time-dependent velocity field that transports the (near-Gaussian) terminal law \(p_T\) of the forward process into the data distribution. Once the field is known, samples can be generated deterministically, by solving an ordinary differential equation.

title: The Probability-Flow ODE
text:
Two conventions: a dictionary
A warning before any formulas. The W01–W02 tutorials used the variance-exploding (VE) convention,
\[
x_\sigma = x_0 + \sigma z ,
\]
in which the clean signal is never rescaled and the variance grows without bound. This tutorial uses the variance-preserving (VP) convention standard in the DDPM literature, in which the signal is simultaneously attenuated:
\[
x_t = \alpha_t\, x_0 + \sigma_t\, \varepsilon,
\qquad \alpha_t^2 + \sigma_t^2 = 1 .
\]
The two are the same construction in different coordinates. The exact dictionary, valid whenever \(\alpha_t > 0\):
\[
\boxed{\;
\begin{aligned}
Y_t &= \frac{X_t}{\alpha_t} = X_0 + \tilde\sigma_t\, \varepsilon,
\qquad
\tilde\sigma_t^2 = \frac{\sigma_t^2}{\alpha_t^2} = \frac{1}{\alpha_t^2} - 1, \\[2pt]
s_Y(y, t) &= \alpha_t\, s_X(\alpha_t y,\, t)
\end{aligned}
\;}
\]
i.e. dividing the VP state by \(\alpha_t\) yields exactly a VE process at noise scale \(\tilde\sigma_t = \sigma_t/\alpha_t\) (the noise-to-signal ratio: with the usual \(\mathrm{SNR} = \alpha^2/\sigma^2\), this is \(\mathrm{SNR}^{-1/2}\)), and scores transform by the chain rule. VP is VE followed by a deterministic shrink.
One caution about a tempting shortcut. For static identities — the corruption formula, the posterior, the denoiser, Tweedie — setting \(\alpha_t = 1\) in a VP expression recovers the corresponding VE formula from W01–W02, and we use this check repeatedly below. For dynamics the shortcut fails: \(\alpha \equiv 1\) in VP forces \(\beta \equiv 0\), a frozen process. The dynamical bridge is the coordinate change above, not a parameter setting.

title: The Probability-Flow ODE
section: The forward SDE, and what it constructs
text:
The forward SDE, and what it constructs
A general diffusion process is specified by a stochastic differential equation
\[
\boxed{\ dX_t = f(X_t, t)\, dt + g(t)\, dW_t \ }
\]
with four ingredients: the state \(X_t \in \mathbb{R}^d\) (the sample at noise level \(t\), with \(X_0 \sim p_{\text{data}}\)); the time \(t \in [0, T]\), which is not physical time but a continuous corruption index; the drift \(f(x,t)\), the deterministic part of the motion (remove the noise term and the dynamics would be \(\dot X = f(X,t)\)); and the diffusion coefficient \(g(t)\) scaling the Brownian increments \(W_{t + dt} - W_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, dt\, I)\) — how much fresh noise is injected per unit of forward time.
The VP diffusion is the choice
\[
\boxed{\ dX_t = -\tfrac12 \beta(t)\, X_t\, dt + \sqrt{\beta(t)}\, dW_t \ }
\]
\[
f(x,t) = -\tfrac12\beta(t)\, x, \qquad g(t) = \sqrt{\beta(t)},
\]
where \(\beta(t) > 0\) is the noise schedule — the only coefficient choice within this VP family: it fixes the drift, the diffusion coefficient, and (below) the corruption parameters. Small \(\beta\) means slow corruption; the usual schedules increase \(\beta(t)\) so that early times perturb gently and late times destroy aggressively.
The name variance-preserving records a covariance identity. From the closed form below, \(\operatorname{Cov}(X_t) = \alpha_t^2 \operatorname{Cov}(X_0) +
(1 - \alpha_t^2) I\): any data law with unit covariance keeps covariance \(I\) for all \(t\) (and if \(X_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)\), the entire law is stationary). For general data the intermediate laws are not Gaussian, but the variance scale stays controlled, and the law approaches \(\mathcal{N}(0, I)\) insofar as \(\alpha_t \to 0\).
The VP SDE admits a closed-form conditional description — for each fixed \(t\),
\[
\boxed{\ X_t \overset{d}{=} \alpha_t X_0 + \sigma_t \varepsilon, \qquad
\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I) \text{ independent of } X_0 \ }
\]
\[
\alpha_t = \exp\!\Big(\!-\tfrac12 \int_0^t \beta(s)\, ds\Big),
\qquad \sigma_t^2 = 1 - \alpha_t^2 .
\]
(This is a distributional identity per time slice; a single fixed \(\varepsilon\) does not describe the joint law of the whole path — for that, the SDE itself is the object.) At \(t = 0\): \(\alpha_0 = 1\), \(\sigma_0 = 0\) — the data itself. As \(t\) grows, \(\alpha_t \to 0\) exactly when \(\int_0^t \beta \to \infty\); at any finite \(T\) with finite \(\int_0^T \beta\), \(\alpha_T\) is small but positive, and \(p_T \approx \mathcal{N}(0, I)\) is an approximation — a good one for standard schedules, and the first entry in the error inventory kept below.






The forward process is a construction, not a destruction



What the forward process constructs is more important than what it destroys: a continuous family of distributions
\[
p_0 = p_{\text{data}}
\;\longrightarrow\; p_t \;\longrightarrow\; p_T \approx \mathcal{N}(0, I),
\]
\[
p_t(x) = \int \mathcal{N}\big(x;\, \alpha_t x_0,\, \sigma_t^2 I\big)\,
p_0(dx_0)
\]
— the rescaled data law convolved with \(\mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_t^2 I)\). Every later object of the theory — the score, the velocity field, the transport — is a property of this family, not of any single noisy sample.


(Writing \(p_0(dx_0)\) matters: the two-point example below has an atomic \(p_0\) with no density.) This family is the path along which the model will later transport probability mass; it is the VP version of the family \(\{p_\sigma\}\) whose 1-D portrait fills the W01–W02 demos. Note that the family depends jointly on the schedule and on \(p_{\text{data}}\): the schedule fixes the corruption kernel, the data fixes what gets corrupted.

title: The Probability-Flow ODE
text:
The score
For each intermediate distribution at \(t > 0\) (where \(p_t\) is a genuine smooth density, whatever \(p_0\) was), define the score:
\[
\boxed{\ s_t(x) = \nabla_x \log p_t(x). \ }
\]
Geometrically: read the density as a landscape; the score points uphill, toward locally more probable samples. It is local information only — a direction, not a destination. Two canonical computations:

Gaussian: for \(p = \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2 I)\), \(\nabla_x \log p(x) = -(x - \mu)/\sigma^2\), pointing at the mean; for \(\mathcal{N}(0, I)\), simply \(-x\).
The two-bump mixture of W01, whose score \(\big(\tanh(x/\sigma^2) - x\big)/\sigma^2\) you have already derived and watched drive the reverse flow.

Here is the crux of the learning problem. The conditional corruption law \(p_t(x_t \mid x_0) = \mathcal{N}(\alpha_t x_0, \sigma_t^2 I)\) is fully known — the schedule fixed it. But the marginal \(p_t\) mixes the conditional over the unknown \(p_{\text{data}}\), so its score cannot be evaluated. The score is the only learned time-dependent function this sampler requires (the exact terminal law \(p_T\) also depends on the data, but it is approximated by a Gaussian rather than learned).

title: The Probability-Flow ODE
text:
Learning the score
Three objects must be kept distinct in this section; conflating any two of them is a standard error.
Object 1: the sampled conditional target. The forward process manufactures training data: draw \(x_0 \sim p_{\text{data}}\), a time \(t\) (from a range bounded away from \(0\), or with a weight that keeps the objective finite — see below), and \(\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)\); form \(x_t = \alpha_t x_0 + \sigma_t
\varepsilon\). The conditional score is analytically available:
\[
\nabla_{x_t} \log p_t(x_t \mid x_0)
= -\frac{x_t - \alpha_t x_0}{\sigma_t^2}
= -\frac{\varepsilon}{\sigma_t}.
\]
This is a random target, different for every draw.
Object 2: the marginal score — the posterior mean of the target. Denoising score matching trains a network \(s_\theta(x, t)\) against Object 1:
\[
\boxed{\
\mathcal{L}(\theta)
= \mathbb{E}\left[ \lambda(t)\,
\Big\| s_\theta(x_t, t) + \frac{\varepsilon}{\sigma_t} \Big\|^2 \right],
\ }
\]
with \(\lambda(t) > 0\) a weighting choice. The reason this works: for each fixed \((x, t)\) with \(t > 0\), the minimizer of a conditional squared error is the conditional mean, and (differentiating under the integral)
\[
\begin{aligned}
s^\star(x, t)
&= \mathbb{E}\big[ \nabla_x \log p_t(x \mid x_0) \,\big|\, x_t = x \big]
= \frac{\int \nabla_x p_t(x \mid x_0)\, p_0(dx_0)}{p_t(x)} \\[2pt]
&= \frac{\nabla_x p_t(x)}{p_t(x)}
= \nabla_x \log p_t(x).
\end{aligned}
\]
The population minimizer over unrestricted functions is the marginal score; a neural network approximates it within its class. (Module 4 does this with full care — Vincent’s identity. Note also that with \(\lambda \equiv 1\) the target variance behaves like \(1/\sigma_t^2\) near \(t = 0\), which is why practical recipes either weight or avoid the smallest times.)
Object 3: the noise-predictor parameterization. Many implementations train \(\varepsilon_\theta(x_t, t)\) to predict the injected noise. Its population optimum is the posterior mean \(\varepsilon^\star(x, t) = \mathbb{E}[\varepsilon
\mid x_t = x]\) — not the per-sample \(\varepsilon\) — and the two optima are linked by
\[
s^\star(x, t) = -\frac{\varepsilon^\star(x, t)}{\sigma_t},
\qquad\text{hence one trains with}\qquad
s_\theta = -\frac{\varepsilon_\theta}{\sigma_t}.
\]
Score prediction and noise prediction are the same estimator in different units; a score loss with weight \(\lambda(t)\) equals a noise loss with weight \(\lambda(t)/\sigma_t^2\).






“Noise prediction” is conditional-mean estimation



The account above is the standard one and its algebra is correct — but the phrase “the network predicts the injected noise”, read literally, is misleading, and it quietly breeds specific misconceptions (collected at the end of this box, each traced to its root). Nor is the phrase a strawman: it is the research literature’s own language, verbatim. The DDPM paper introduces the network as “a function approximator intended to predict \(\varepsilon\) from \(\mathbf{x}_t\)”1; the DDIM paper writes that “the model \(\varepsilon_\theta^{(t)}(\mathbf{x}_t)\) then attempts to predict \(\varepsilon_t\) from \(\mathbf{x}_t\), without knowledge of \(\mathbf{x}_0\)”2; Nichol and Dhariwal state that “the network could also predict the noise \(\varepsilon\)” and that “predicting \(\varepsilon\) worked best”3. The expository canon carries it further: the widely used Hugging Face implementation guide describes the reparametrization as making “the neural network learn (predict) the added noise” and concludes that “our neural network becomes a noise predictor, rather than a (direct) mean predictor”4 — a phrasing worth savoring, since the population-optimal noise predictor is a mean predictor, of the conditional kind. Careful statements do exist in print — the tutorial of Nakkiran et al. presents \(\varepsilon\)-, \(x_0\)-, and \(v\)-prediction uniformly as estimation of conditional expectations5 — but they are the exception, not the phrasing that spread. The phrasing is harmless to authors who hold the algebra in their heads — and misleading to every reader who does not. (One terminological note: throughout, \(\varepsilon\) denotes the aggregate noise of the fixed-\(t\) representation \(x_t = \alpha_t x_0 + \sigma_t \varepsilon\) — the object the literature’s phrase refers to — not the one-step innovation between adjacent times.)
\[
\varepsilon
= \underbrace{\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon \mid x_t, t]}_{\displaystyle \varepsilon^\star(x_t, t)}
+ \underbrace{\big(\varepsilon - \mathbb{E}[\varepsilon \mid x_t, t]\big)}_{\text{zero conditional mean}} ,
\]
the first term a deterministic function of what the network sees, the second a residual with zero conditional mean (not independent of the observation — only its best point prediction is exhausted). For any predictor that is a function of \((x_t, t)\), the tower property splits the loss accordingly:
\[
\mathbb{E}\big\|\varepsilon_\theta - \varepsilon\big\|^2
= \mathbb{E}\big\|\varepsilon_\theta - \varepsilon^\star\big\|^2
+ \underbrace{\mathbb{E}\big\|\varepsilon - \varepsilon^\star\big\|^2}_{\text{irreducible floor}}
\]
(a time-dependent weight \(\lambda(t)\) multiplies both terms alike). Only the first term is reducible in population risk. The floor equals \(\mathbb{E}\, \operatorname{tr} \operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon \mid x_t, t)\) — the minimum mean-squared error — and for nondegenerate data at finite noise levels it is strictly positive: the training loss does not approach zero, and should not.
The reducible part is an object we have already met:
\[
\varepsilon^\star(x, t) = -\sigma_t\, s_t(x)
\]
— the negative, \(\sigma_t\)-scaled score. The predictable component of the noise encodes exactly the score, and nothing more. Equivalently, in displacement form: \(\sigma_t\, \varepsilon^\star(x,t) = x - \alpha_t\, \mathbb{E}[X_0 \mid x]
= -\sigma_t^2 s_t(x)\) — the posterior-mean offset of the observation from the attenuated clean signal (a mean, not a most-likely value). It is a deterministic, smoothly varying field: for the two-point example below, \(\varepsilon^\star(x,t) = \big(x - \alpha_t \tanh(\alpha_t x/\sigma_t^2)\big)/\sigma_t\), a smooth curve in \(x\).
The confusion has a simple source. In a regression there are two different objects: the target — the random quantity each training pair happens to contain (here, the sampled \(\varepsilon\)) — and the fitted function — what the trained model actually computes, namely the average of all targets compatible with a given input (here, \(\varepsilon^\star\)). The phrase “noise prediction” names the target; the network is the fitted function. In careful regression language the phrase is even defensible — predicting a random target means estimating its conditional mean — but the colloquial reading of “noise” hides that this is what is happening.
Two consequences sharpen the picture.

Structure in the data appears as the nonlinear part of the conditional-mean field — and that field, not any randomness, is what the network learns. For data with no data-specific structure (\(p_{\text{data}} = \mathcal{N}(0, I)\), so \(p_t = \mathcal{N}(0, I)\) and \(s_t(x) = -x\)), the field reduces to the linear baseline \(\varepsilon^\star = \sigma_t x\); in the probability-flow ODE this score exactly cancels the VP drift — zero velocity, nothing to transport.
How much of the noise is predictable depends on the data and the noise level. For smooth, full-dimensional data, \(\mathbb{E}\|\varepsilon^\star\|^2 = \sigma_t^2\, J(p_t) \to 0\) as \(\sigma_t \to 0\) (with \(J\) the Fisher information): the standardized noise becomes mostly unpredictable even though denoising is easy. For atomic or well-separated data — the two-point example — the nearby atom becomes identifiable at small \(\sigma_t\) and the noise becomes nearly recoverable from the observation. At the other extreme (\(\sigma_t \to 1\), \(\alpha_t \to 0\)), \(x_t \to \varepsilon\) and prediction is trivial: the observation mostly is the noise.

The root cause, and the three misconceptions it breeds. Each falsehood below is a logical consequence of taking “the network predicts the noise” literally; each is followed by the correcting fact.

If the noise can truly be predicted, the training loss should reach zero. — In fact the loss is bounded below by \(\mathbb{E}\, \operatorname{tr} \operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon \mid x_t, t) > 0\) for nondegenerate data at finite noise level; no function of \((x_t, t)\) can go beneath it.
If what is being predicted is “noise”, the prediction should look like static and jitter. — In fact the fitted function is a deterministic field: evaluated twice at the same \((x_t, t)\) it returns the same answer, and it varies smoothly with its input — the two-point formula above is a \(\tanh\) curve, not a jitter. (Its values can occasionally resemble a noise pattern — for Gaussian data \(\varepsilon^\star = \sigma_t x_t\) — but it is a fixed function of the input, never a fresh random draw.)
If the network predicts noise, it has the strange ability to predict randomness. — In fact it estimates a conditional mean: the structured component \(\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon \mid x_t, t]\), the part of the noise that the observation determines. The genuinely random residual is never predicted by anything.

title: The Probability-Flow ODE
section: From SDE to ODE: the derivation
text:
From SDE to ODE: the derivation
This is the heart of the tutorial. The density of the forward SDE evolves by the Fokker–Planck equation (Module 5 derives it; here we use it):
\[
\boxed{\
\frac{\partial p_t}{\partial t}
= -\nabla \cdot (f\, p_t) + \tfrac12 g(t)^2\, \Delta p_t
\ }
\]
— deterministic transport by the drift, plus spreading by the noise. Separately, purely deterministic particle motion \(\dot X_t = v(X_t, t)\) evolves its density by the continuity equation:
\[
\frac{\partial p_t}{\partial t} = -\nabla \cdot (p_t\, v).
\]
The question writes itself: is there a velocity field \(v\) whose noiseless transport reproduces exactly the density evolution of the noisy SDE? Try
\[
v(x, t) = f(x, t) - \tfrac12 g(t)^2\, \nabla_x \log p_t(x).
\]
Then, using \(p_t \nabla \log p_t = \nabla p_t\),
\[
p_t v = p_t f - \tfrac12 g^2\, p_t \nabla \log p_t
      = p_t f - \tfrac12 g^2\, \nabla p_t,
\]
so
\[
-\nabla \cdot (p_t v)
= -\nabla \cdot (p_t f) + \tfrac12 g^2\, \nabla \cdot (\nabla p_t)
= -\nabla \cdot (p_t f) + \tfrac12 g^2\, \Delta p_t
\]
— exactly the Fokker–Planck right-hand side. The diffusion term has been absorbed into an extra drift along the score (in forward time the correction points down the score, spreading mass; integrated backward it points up). Hence the deterministic dynamics
\[
\boxed{\
\frac{dX_t}{dt} = f(X_t, t) - \tfrac12 g(t)^2\, \nabla_x \log p_t(X_t)
\ }
\]
reproduces the marginals \(p_t\) on any interval \([\epsilon, T]\) with \(\epsilon > 0\), when initialized from the matching law at either end (from \(p_T\), integrated backward, for generation). If \(p_0\) itself is singular — the two-point example — the flow reaches it only in the \(\epsilon \downarrow 0\) limit: a smooth flow cannot terminate on atoms at any positive time, which is the VP face of the \(\sigma_{\min}\) discussion in the earlier tutorials. This is the probability-flow ODE. For VP diffusion it takes a compact form:
\[
\boxed{\
\frac{dX_t}{dt} = -\tfrac12 \beta(t)\, \big[ X_t + s_t(X_t) \big],
\ }
\]
and with the learned score, \(s_t \to s_\theta\). (In \(d > 1\) this velocity is the canonical choice, not the unique one: adding any field \(u\) with \(\nabla\!\cdot(p_t u) = 0\) preserves the same marginals. In one dimension the monotone flow is unique — the rigidity used below.)
One box on the stochastic alternative, for completeness. Introduce the increasing reverse clock \(\tau = T - t\), so that “later” means “less noisy”; then the same score defines the reverse-time SDE
\[
dX = \big[ -f(X, t) + g(t)^2\, s_t(X) \big]\, d\tau + g(t)\, d\bar W_\tau ,
\]
with \(\bar W\) a fresh Brownian motion in the \(\tau\) clock. Note the score coefficient \(g^2\) — twice the ODE’s \(\tfrac12 g^2\) — compensating the re-injected noise: the same doubling you saw in the two-point sampler of W01. With the exact score and exact initialization from \(p_T\), both samplers traverse the same family \(\{p_t\}\); the ODE is deterministic given \(X_T\), the SDE consumes fresh randomness at every instant. From here on we follow the ODE.
Two readings of the result:

Kinematic: the equation is first-order — it prescribes velocity, not force. Every point of space-time carries an arrow \(v(x,t)\); a particle follows the arrow under its feet, and the arrows change both because the particle moves and because the field is time-dependent.
Hydrodynamic: release many particles from \(p_T\) and let each follow the field; individually deterministic, collectively their density flows — the continuity equation is conservation of probability mass. Hence the name: probability flows through space under a deterministic velocity field.

And the answer to a question worth asking out loud: is the score the velocity? No. The velocity is drift plus score correction,
\[
v = \underbrace{f}_{\text{known from the schedule}}
- \underbrace{\tfrac12 g^2\, s}_{\text{learned correction}},
\]
with the schedule deciding how strongly the learned geometry steers the motion.

title: The Probability-Flow ODE
text:
Sampling is numerical integration
After training, everything on the right-hand side of the ODE is available: the schedule supplies \(\beta(t)\) — hence \(f\), \(g\), \(\alpha_t\), \(\sigma_t\) — and the network supplies \(s_\theta(x, t)\). Generation is: draw \(X_T \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)\) (the Gaussian stand-in for \(p_T\)), integrate backward to \(t = \epsilon\), return the endpoint. But the trajectory is defined implicitly — \(v\) depends on the state along the unknown path — so for a neural score there is generally no closed form. The trajectory is computed numerically.
Fix a descending grid \(T = t_N > t_{N-1} > \cdots > t_1 > t_0 = \epsilon\), with \(h_k = t_{k-1} - t_k < 0\) (backward steps), and \(\epsilon > 0\) a small final time. The Euler sampler:
\[
\boxed{\
\begin{aligned}
&X \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I) \\
&\text{for } k = N, N-1, \dots, 1: \\
&\qquad s \leftarrow s_\theta(X, t_k) \\
&\qquad v \leftarrow -\tfrac12 \beta(t_k)\, (X + s) \\
&\qquad X \leftarrow X + h_k\, v \\
&\text{return } X
\end{aligned}
\ }
\]
Since \(h_k < 0\), the score increment is \(+\tfrac12 \beta(t_k)\, |h_k|\,
s_\theta\) — the particle steps up the score, consistent with W01’s sampler. Four remarks that carry more weight than the pseudocode:

The score must be re-evaluated at every step. Both of its arguments change: the particle moved, and the noise level dropped. Each step is evaluate score → construct velocity → move → repeat — the sampler incrementally reconstructs a global transport from local information.
Better integrators exist. Heun’s method: take the provisional Euler step \(X^* = X_k + h_k\, v(X_k, t_k)\), re-evaluate the velocity at the provisional state and the new time, \(v^* = v(X^*, t_{k-1})\), then move by the average, \(X_{k-1} = X_k + \tfrac{h_k}{2}\big( v(X_k, t_k) + v^* \big)\) — second-order accuracy (for sufficiently smooth fields) at two network calls per step. Beyond it: Runge–Kutta, adaptive solvers, multistep and diffusion-specific schemes. The relevant cost metric is the number of neural function evaluations (NFE), since each velocity evaluation runs the network once.
The four errors, inventoried (mirroring the W01 tutorial’s honesty paragraph): (i) terminal-prior mismatch — sampling \(\mathcal{N}(0, I)\) instead of the true \(p_T\); (ii) score error — \(s_\theta \ne s_t\); (iii) integration error — finite steps; (iv) finite-\(\epsilon\) endpoint bias — stopping at \(t = \epsilon\). Under exact prior, exact score, and exact integration, the endpoint law is exactly \(p_\epsilon\); the practical sampler carries all four deviations.
The \(\epsilon\)-endpoint is not a technicality. Even the idealized endpoint \(p_\epsilon\) is the attenuated and smoothed data law (\(\alpha_\epsilon X_0 + \sigma_\epsilon Z\)), not the data law itself — the VP twin of the terminal width \(\sigma_{\min}\) quantified in the W01 tutorial and The Deterministic Map, Proved. Increasing the step count removes integration error only; lowering \(\epsilon\) sharpens the target, at the price of an increasingly stiff velocity field (for the two-point score below, the derivative at the separatrix scales like \(\sigma_t^{-4}\)).

title: The Probability-Flow ODE
section: The two-point example, in VP coordinates
text:
The two-point example, in VP coordinates
Now run the entire pipeline on the course’s home dataset, \(p_0 = \tfrac12 \delta_{-1} + \tfrac12 \delta_{+1}\) — the case where every learned object has a formula, worked in the VE convention in the W01 tutorial and proved in The Deterministic Map, Proved. Conditioning on the component, \(X_t \mid X_0 = \pm 1 \sim \mathcal{N}(\pm\alpha_t, \sigma_t^2)\), so
\[
p_t(x) = \tfrac12\, \mathcal{N}(x; -\alpha_t, \sigma_t^2)
       + \tfrac12\, \mathcal{N}(x; +\alpha_t, \sigma_t^2)
\]
(sanity check: \(\operatorname{Var}(X_t) = \alpha_t^2 + \sigma_t^2 = 1\) — variance preserved exactly). The posterior is one line of Bayes — the likelihood ratio of the two components is \(\exp(-2\alpha_t x/\sigma_t^2)\), so
\[
\mathbb{P}(X_0 = +1 \mid X_t = x)
= \operatorname{sigmoid}\!\Big( \frac{2 \alpha_t x}{\sigma_t^2} \Big),
\]
\[
\widehat X_0(x, t) := \mathbb{E}[X_0 \mid X_t = x]
= \tanh\!\Big( \frac{\alpha_t x}{\sigma_t^2} \Big),
\]
and the score follows in one more line from VP Tweedie (\(s = (\alpha_t\, \mathbb{E}[X_0 \mid x] - x)/\sigma_t^2\), derived in the next section):
\[
s_t(x) = \frac{ \alpha_t \tanh(\alpha_t x / \sigma_t^2) - x }{ \sigma_t^2 },
\]
\[
v_t(x) = -\tfrac12 \beta(t)
\left[ x + \frac{ \alpha_t \tanh(\alpha_t x/\sigma_t^2) - x }{ \sigma_t^2 } \right].
\]
Setting \(\alpha_t = 1\) recovers every corresponding W01 formula — the static dictionary at work. As \(t \to 0\): \(\alpha_t \to 1\), \(\sigma_t \to 0\), so \(\widehat X_0(x, t) \to \operatorname{sign}(x)\) pointwise for \(x \ne 0\) (not uniformly near \(0\)) — the smooth \(\tanh\) denoiser sharpening into the discontinuous sign map.
What does the integrated flow do? The 1-D argument of The Deterministic Map, Proved runs in two stages, and the order matters. Stage one, at positive noise: for each \(\epsilon > 0\), the flow map \(\Psi_{T \to \epsilon}\) is continuous and strictly increasing (trajectories of a smooth 1-D ODE cannot cross), and a monotone map pushing \(p_T\) to \(p_\epsilon\) is unique — therefore
\[
\Psi_{T \to \epsilon} = F_\epsilon^{-1} \circ F_T ,
\]
the quantile transport between the two mixture CDFs. (At finite \(T\), \(F_T\) is the CDF of the near-Gaussian mixture, not of \(\mathcal{N}(0,1)\); by symmetry both place their median at \(0\), which is all the limit needs.) Stage two, the limit: as \(\epsilon \downarrow 0\), the target collapses onto the atoms and
\[
\boxed{\ \Psi_{T \to \epsilon}(X_T) \;\longrightarrow\; \operatorname{sign}(X_T)
\qquad p_T\text{-almost surely}. \ }
\]
Every positive start ends at \(+1\), every negative start at \(-1\), and symmetry sends exactly half the mass to each atom. For the smoothed target \(\tfrac12\mathcal{N}(-1, \varrho^2) + \tfrac12\mathcal{N}(+1, \varrho^2)\) the finite-\(T\) endpoint map is the genuine quantile transport \(F_{0,\varrho}^{-1} \circ F_T\) (which becomes \(F_{0,\varrho}^{-1} \circ \Phi\) only in the idealized exactly-Gaussian-terminal limit), converging to the sign map as \(\varrho \to 0\).
One qualification keeps the example honest. In this special symmetric case the endpoint of the flow happens to be a formula we could have written down without any ODE. The solver is not “numerically approximating the sign function” in general: it solves a differential equation whose endpoint, for arbitrary data, is not known in advance — that is the entire point of learning the score.

title: The Probability-Flow ODE
section: Three distinctions that prevent three confusions
text:
Three distinctions that prevent three confusions
The score is not the velocity. \(v = f - \tfrac12 g^2 s\): the learned score is the correction; the schedule contributes the drift and decides the correction’s strength.
The denoiser is not the endpoint. VP Tweedie (set \(\alpha \equiv 1\) to recover W01’s version) gives the one-step posterior mean
\[
\mathbb{E}[X_0 \mid X_t = x] = \frac{x + \sigma_t^2\, s_t(x)}{\alpha_t}
\qquad (\alpha_t > 0),
\]
a single denoising estimate from noise level \(t\). The flow endpoint \(\Psi_{T \to \epsilon}(X_T)\) integrates the score field through every level. In the two-point limit both converge to the same sign decision — because a trajectory that never touches \(0\) keeps its sign, and the denoiser’s sign at any level agrees with it — but they are different objects, and conflating them is a common reading error in the literature.
The one-shot map and the incremental flow solve the same problem. Define the per-step Euler map \(E_k(x) = x + h_k\, v(x, t_k)\). Then the endpoint transport is represented implicitly as a time-ordered composition,
\[
\Psi_{T \to \epsilon}
= \lim_{\max_k |h_k| \to 0}\; E_1 \circ E_2 \circ \cdots \circ E_N ,
\]
— the factorization view of The Deterministic Map, Proved, now with a learned field: each factor is near-identity and needs only local information. For fixed \(\epsilon > 0\) this limit is a continuous map; any discontinuity (the sign function) arises only in the separate limit \(\epsilon \downarrow 0\).

title: The Probability-Flow ODE
The Probability-Flow ODE
text:
Takeaways

The schedule \(\beta(t)\) determines the corruption kernel — drift, diffusion coefficient, \(\alpha_t\), \(\sigma_t\); together with the data it determines the family \(\{p_t\}\).
The score \(\nabla \log p_t\) is the only learned time-dependent function the sampler needs, trained by denoising score matching on synthetically corrupted data; noise prediction is the same estimator in different units, with population optimum \(-\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon \mid x_t]/\sigma_t\).
The probability-flow ODE replaces the SDE’s noise by an extra drift along the score, reproducing the same marginals deterministically on \([\epsilon, T]\): \(v = f - \tfrac12 g^2 s\).
Sampling is numerical ODE integration; each step is score evaluation → velocity → move; accuracy is bought with NFE; and the practical sampler carries four distinct errors — prior mismatch, score error, integration error, and the finite-\(\epsilon\) endpoint bias.
In the two-point limit the integrated flow converges to the sign map — locally learned gradients, integrated into a transport that is discontinuous only in the \(\epsilon \downarrow 0\) limit — and for real data the same principle holds with no formula available: the global generative transformation is obtained by integrating locally learned score information.

title: The Probability-Flow ODE
text:
Exercises

(One-dimensional.) Verify from the closed form \(X_t \overset{d}{=} \alpha_t X_0 + \sigma_t \varepsilon\) that \(\operatorname{Var}(X_t) = \alpha_t^2 \operatorname{Var}(X_0) + \sigma_t^2\), and confirm the variance-preserving property for unit-variance data. State the \(d\)-dimensional covariance version.
Use the static dictionary (\(\alpha \equiv 1\)) to recover, from the VP two-point formulas: the mixture \(p_t\), the posterior, the denoiser, and the score — and match each against the W01 tutorial. Then use the dynamic dictionary (\(Y = X/\alpha\)) to transform the VP score into the VE score and check consistency.
Complete the proof that the population minimizer of the denoising score-matching objective is the marginal score, stating explicitly where \(t > 0\), \(\lambda(t) > 0\), and differentiation under the integral are used.
Show that the reverse-time SDE and the probability-flow ODE differ exactly by replacing \(\tfrac12 g^2 s\, dt\) with \(g^2 s\, dt - g\, d\bar W\), and argue via the Fokker–Planck equation that both preserve the family \(\{p_t\}\) under exact score and exact terminal initialization.
A reproducible benchmark. Take \(\beta(t) = 0.1 + 19.9\,t\) on \([0, 1]\) (so \(\alpha_t = e^{-(0.05 t + 4.975 t^2)}\)), \(\epsilon = 10^{-3}\), a uniform grid in \(t\), exact two-point score, and \(X_T \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)\). Measure the RMS distance of endpoints to the nearest atom. Compare Euler and Heun at equal NFE (Euler gets twice the steps). Which wins at NFE = 10? At NFE = 100?
For the smoothed two-point target with component variance \(\varrho^2\), write the VP forward family \(p_t\) explicitly (hint: Gaussians convolve), and verify that the finite-\(T\) quantile transport is \(F_{0,\varrho}^{-1} \circ F_T\), reducing to \(F_{0,\varrho}^{-1} \circ \Phi\) only when \(p_T\) is replaced by its Gaussian idealization.
For the two-point score, compute \(s_t'(0)\) and show it scales as \(\alpha_t^2/\sigma_t^4\) for small \(\sigma_t\) — the stiffness quoted in the sampling section. Where in \(x\) is \(|s_t'|\) largest, and why is that exactly where a numerical integrator needs small steps?
